lessons.title: Use AI Safely Once
lessons.coreQuestion: How can I use an AI assistant without handing over my privacy, voice, or final decision?
lessons.blurb: Make several realistic choices, see what the system is actually doing, and leave with one control rule you can use immediately.

steps.title: AI is already inside ordinary decisions
steps.scenario:
A group chat says school is closed tomorrow. The screenshot looks official, but nobody links the source. Someone asks you to repost it. An AI assistant could rewrite the announcement, explain the screenshot, or confidently tell you it is real—but none of those actions proves the claim. Before learning how a model works, you need a way to keep control of what happens next.

This lesson is not graded. Use made-up examples. Do not enter a real name, school, address, password, private message, health detail, or another person's information.
steps.prompt: What would matter most before you shared the announcement: speed, confidence, or evidence that tomorrow's closure is current? Hold your answer; you will test it next.

steps.title: Choose the kind of control each moment needs
steps.prompt: These are not trivia questions. They are small decisions people make while using AI. Sort each next move by the control it protects; retry any choice without penalty.

items.text: Ask for three possible titles, then choose and rewrite one in your own voice.
Confirm tonight's opening hours on the venue's official page before your friend travels.
Describe an argument without names or screenshots before asking for calmer reply ideas.
Compare several possible plans, then let the people involved make the final choice.
Verify a specific number with a current independent source before acting on it.
Replace a real location and personal details with an invented example before typing.

steps.reveal: You just used three different controls: AI can generate options, outside evidence checks consequential facts, and redaction protects the people inside the prompt.

steps.title: The output is only one part of the system
steps.body:
When you type into an AI product, five parts are involved: you bring a goal; the app receives your request; a model predicts a response from patterns and context; optional tools may add search, files, memory, or calculations; and then you decide whether to edit, reject, verify, or act. The model does not receive the consequence if the answer is wrong. You and the people affected do.

That is why safety comes before technical detail. A fluent answer can be useful material, but it is not permission to share private information or proof that a current claim is true. The machine produces an output. Human judgment turns—or refuses to turn—that output into action.
steps.mistake: Treating the chatbot as one all-knowing object, then assuming its polished answer has already completed the checking and deciding for you.
steps.good: Name the job you are giving AI, remove information it does not need, and keep the final check and decision with a person.

steps.title: Context changes the prediction
steps.strong: Write three short ways to tell a close friend I cannot come tonight. Keep the tone warm, do not invent a reason, and leave the final wording for me to choose.
steps.why: The model predicts from the words and context it receives. Clear audience, limits, and purpose change the likely output. Better context improves fit; it still does not make an invented claim true or make the final choice for you.

steps.goal: Use AI to help plan a group meetup without exposing private information or treating a likely answer as a verified plan.

State the goal and limits
Ask for several options
Check current facts independently
Let the people involved decide
choices: Ask for several options
Check current facts independently
Let the people involved decide
Remove private details
State the goal and limits
steps.note: The order matters. Protect people before typing, define the real task, use prediction for options, verify the current details that change the plan, and keep the consequence with the humans involved.

steps.title: Make the whole decision
steps.question: A friend sends you a private group-chat screenshot and asks AI to plan a meetup from it. The answer suggests a venue with exact prices and opening hours. Which complete next move keeps the tool useful without giving it control?

options.text: Paste the screenshot because exact personal context will make the plan more accurate, then follow the most confident answer.
options.feedback: More private context is not automatically safer or necessary, and confidence is not evidence that current venue details are correct.

options.text: Remove names and private details, state the group's real constraints, use AI for options, verify current venue facts, and let the group decide.
options.feedback: That combines privacy, useful context, independent verification, and human decision-making. AI helps without owning the consequence.

options.text: Ask the same AI to cite itself and promise the prices are current before sending the plan to everyone.
options.feedback: A stronger promise from the same system is still not independent evidence. Check the venue's current information outside the chatbot.

options.text: Never use AI for planning because any mistake means the tool is useless.
options.feedback: That avoids the risk by losing the benefit. The stronger skill is deciding what AI can help with and what a person must protect, check, and decide.

lessons.title: What Is Actually Happening
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI gives you an answer, what are the pieces behind it, and which part is still your job?
lessons.blurb: See the few simple parts behind any AI answer, so you always know which part you still decide.

steps.title: The answer came fast. The choice is still yours.
steps.scenario:
You ask an app when the last bus leaves. It says 10:40 p.m.

You need that bus to get home. The screen looks confident. But you cannot tell if it read today's timetable, or if it is repeating something it saw months ago.
steps.prompt: What would you want to know before you plan your night around 10:40?

steps.title: Which part is doing each job?
steps.prompt: Sort each job. Get it wrong as often as you like — the point is to see the parts, not one magic box.

items.text: Sets the goal: get home safely
Provides the chat or search screen
Predicts a useful-looking response from the context
Looks up a live transport timetable when available
Checks the official schedule and chooses what to do

steps.reveal: The app is the surface, the model predicts the response, and a tool may fetch current information. None of those parts receives the consequence if the bus time is wrong. The person checks and decides.

steps.title: Four parts, and you are the last one
steps.body:
An AI answer is not one magic box. It is a few parts working together.

The app is the thing you type into. A website, a keyboard, a chat box, a game.

The guesser is the part that writes the answer. People call it a model. It has read an enormous amount of writing, and it guesses which words should come next. It is guessing, not looking things up.

Helpers are extras the app can plug in: live search, a calculator, your files. Helpers can fetch real, current facts. The guesser on its own cannot.

You are the last part. You read it, check it if it matters, and decide what to do.

Here is why this matters. The guesser sounds exactly the same whether it checked something or not.
steps.mistake: Calling the whole thing 'the AI' and assuming a polished answer means every hidden part worked correctly.
steps.good: Ask which product, model, data, and tools are involved, then keep the final decision with the person affected.

steps.note: Take private details out before you type. The guesser can lay out the choices. Helpers can add today's real prices. You still make the call.

lessons.title: Change One Clue, Change the Answer
lessons.coreQuestion: Why do the words around your question change the answer, and why can a likely answer still be wrong?
lessons.blurb: Change one clue, watch the answer move, and see why a good guess is not proof.

steps.title: One message, three different endings
steps.scenario:
You start typing: 'I cannot make it tonight because…' Your phone offers to finish it for you.

In the team group chat it offers 'I have a match'. In the family chat it offers 'I feel sick'. In the game chat it offers 'the update is still downloading'.

The start was the same every time. The words around it changed. So the guess changed.
steps.prompt: You are in a chat about a cancelled birthday party. Which ending would your phone offer, and what made you pick it?

steps.title: Which chat does each ending fit?
steps.prompt: Sort each ending by the chat it fits best. More than one could work. Pick the strongest clue.

items.text: …the pan is already smoking.
…the new brake cable arrives on Friday.
…I need a bit of time before we talk.
…the sauce needs ten more minutes.
…my dad said he would pay for the part.
…I do not want this to turn into another argument.

steps.reveal: The AI leans on the words around your question. Change the clues and a different ending fits. That makes the ending more likely. It does not make it true.

steps.title: It builds the answer one word at a time
steps.body:
The part that writes the answer is a guesser. People call it a model.

It has read an enormous amount of writing. Given your words so far, it picks the word that fits best. Then it does that again. And again. That is how a whole answer gets built.

People call this predicting. It only means guessing what comes next.

So the answer arrives one piece at a time. It was never sitting there finished, waiting for you.

Everything around your question is a clue: the earlier messages, the chat you are in, the details you added. People call all those clues together the context.

More clues make the guess fit better. Fitting better is not the same as being right. A homework answer can read beautifully and still be wrong.

This lesson works entirely inside LearningAI. If you do try an outside app, use a made-up example and keep private details out.
steps.mistake: Thinking a smooth paragraph means the AI understands the world the way you do.
steps.good: Use clues to shape the guess, then check the facts yourself before you rely on them.

lessons.title: A Typo Costs Nothing. This Costs a Lot.
lessons.coreQuestion: If a messy message cannot hurt the machine, what can careless use cost me?
lessons.blurb: Type badly without fear. Guard your private details, your time, your voice, and the final call.

steps.title: The typo is harmless. The screenshot is not.
steps.scenario:
A friend sent you a message and you cannot work out what they meant. You want help writing back.

You worry your question is badly written. So you think about pasting in the whole chat, screenshots and all, to give the AI everything.

The typos cannot hurt the AI. Sharing your friend's messages can hurt your friend.
steps.prompt: Which one actually deserves your worry: the messy wording, the private chat, or both? Say why.

steps.title: Just try again, or stop first?
steps.prompt: Sort what you can safely redo from what needs you to stop and think.

items.text: A half-finished sentence full of spelling mistakes
A screenshot of a friend's chat with names and numbers in it
Changing your mind about what you want after seeing the first draft
Letting AI send a message to someone before you have read it
Asking the same question again in simpler words
Spending an hour hunting the perfect answer instead of just deciding

steps.reveal: You cannot hurt the AI's feelings, and a typo breaks nothing. You can leak someone's private messages, lose an hour, lose your own voice, or act on a wrong answer. Worry about the cost, not the sentence.

steps.title: Keep the mess, remove the exposure
steps.weak: help me answer this im confused [whole screenshot of the chat, with names, numbers and where they live]
steps.strong: help me write 3 replies to [a friend]. [what happened in one line]. Keep it [how I want to sound]. Do not invent reasons for what they did. I will pick one and rewrite it.

steps.title: A redo is free. A consequence is not.
steps.body:
The AI writes an answer from whatever words you give it. A messy question may get a messy answer. You can fix that in your next message. Nothing is lost.

Some things do not undo. Your friend's private chat, once pasted, is out. So is money spent, a message sent in the wrong voice, or a decision made from an invented fact.

So before you paste anything into an outside app, swap things out. Real names, real messages, your school, your address, anything about money or health. Use made-up stand-ins instead.

Everything you need for this lesson is right here. You never have to send a real message anywhere to finish it.
steps.mistake: Polishing your sentence while ignoring whose private details are sitting inside it.
steps.good: Send a rough question with the private parts taken out, then check the answer before you act on it.

Say what you actually want, in one line

choices: Ask for a few new versions

options.text: Delete it all and stop using AI, because one bad draft proves it cannot help.
options.feedback: The bad draft costs nothing to redo. Fixing it while holding your boundaries is the real skill.

lessons.title: Check It, Then Decide
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I work out what needs checking, find proof somewhere else, and make the call myself?
lessons.blurb: Turn one confident-sounding answer into a checked decision that you actually own.

steps.title: A confident answer can still send someone the wrong way
steps.scenario:
Your brother has hurt his wrist. Your mum asks you to find out when the walk-in clinic shuts.

An AI says 8 p.m. You would leave at 7:20.

That 8 p.m. could come from an old page, from a live search, or from nothing at all. Asking the AI to sound more sure will not keep the doors open.
steps.prompt: Which exact fact would change what you do, and where could you check it without asking the same AI again?

steps.title: Match the checking to the cost
steps.prompt: Decide how hard each answer needs checking. Not every draft needs an investigation. Not every serious claim can ride on how good it sounds.
buckets: Just read it and use it
AI does not get to decide this

items.text: Three name ideas for a made-up comic character
What time the clinic shuts tonight
Whether a text asking you for a payment is real
Whether someone should stop taking medicine a doctor gave them
A rough first draft of a caption for the team photo
Whether a classmate should be punished for something someone accused them of

steps.reveal: The bigger the cost of being wrong, the harder you check. When health, safety, or someone's name is involved, AI can help you think. It does not get the final say.

steps.title: Build a trail you can show
steps.claim: The clinic shuts at 8 p.m. tonight.
steps: Pick the one fact that changes what you do
Find a source that is actually in charge of that fact
Check the date, the place, and the exact wording
Write down whether it held up, failed, or is still unclear
Decide from the evidence and the cost, not from how sure the AI sounded
steps.note: The clinic's own page or phone line is real proof. Asking the same chatbot 'are you sure?' is not.

steps.title: A useful answer is not proof
steps.body:
The AI writes what fits. Some apps can also run a live search and pull in what they find. Even then, links and quotes need a look. A link can point somewhere that never says what the answer claims.

Checking means testing the claim against something outside that answer. Deciding means weighing what you found against the cost of being wrong, then choosing.

Keep private things out of outside apps. Use a made-up example, or take out names, addresses, account numbers, and health details first.

The claim trail above is enough to finish this lesson on its own.
steps.mistake: Asking the same AI to repeat itself, add links, or sound careful, then calling that proof.
steps.good: Name the fact that matters, check a source that owns it, say honestly how sure you are, and decide yourself.

correct: Do not tap the link or type in any account details
Name the claim: this bill is real and it is urgent
Reach the company a way you already know is real
Compare what they say with what the message said
Decide whether to pay, report it, or ignore it
choices: Compare what they say with what the message said
Decide whether to pay, report it, or ignore it

lessons.title: Where Did This Come From?
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI makes a picture, some writing, or a voice, how can I tell where it really came from?
lessons.blurb: Learn why you cannot tell how something was made just by looking at it, and what to check instead.

steps.title: It looks real. That tells you nothing.
steps.scenario:
You ask an app for a poster of a glass city under two moons. Seconds later, there it is. It looks incredible.

But you cannot tell how the app got it. It might have made the picture itself. It might have found one someone else drew. It might have mixed both together.
steps.prompt: If a friend asked "did the AI actually make that?", what could you honestly say right now?

steps.title: Made or found, and why you cannot see the difference
steps.body:
There are two different things an app can do, and they look identical on screen.

Made means the AI built something new, piece by piece, from patterns it learned. Nobody drew that exact picture before.

Found means the app went and got something that already existed, that a real person made.

Here is the problem. A finished picture cannot tell you which one happened. Looking closer does not help. Neither does it looking impressive.

The only way to know is if the app tells you. Some apps show a link to where something came from, or a small label saying the AI made this. That label is your evidence. The picture itself never is.

If there is no label and no link, the honest answer is "I do not know where this came from". That is a real answer, and it is the right one.
steps.mistake: Assuming that a surprising result proves the assistant generated every part of it from scratch.
steps.good: Ask what system or tool produced the result, what source information is available, and what still needs human checking.

steps.title: What can you honestly say?
steps.prompt: For each one, pick the strongest thing you are allowed to claim. Do not judge by how good it looks.

items.text: The product's activity record says 'image generated' and provides content credentials for this result.
The assistant gives a direct source link to a museum photograph and says it retrieved that exact image.
A strange picture appears with no source, tool label, or creation record.
A quoted paragraph includes a working link to the original article and matches it word for word.
A voice clip sounds like a real person, but there is no label explaining whether it was recorded, cloned, or synthesized.

steps.reveal: Looking good is not evidence. A label or a link tells you where something came from. No label means "I do not know" — and saying that is not a failure.

lessons.title: Sure-Sounding and Still Wrong
lessons.coreQuestion: Why can AI sound totally certain and still be wrong, and what should I do about it?
lessons.blurb: A made-up detail sounds exactly as sure as a true one. You cannot feel the difference. You have to check.

steps.title: The smooth wrong answer
steps.scenario:
You ask an AI about your own town. Back come dates, names and numbers. Smooth, exact, completely sure of itself.

One of those facts is invented. Nothing in the wording gives it away. It reads exactly like the true parts.
steps.prompt: Honest guess before you read on: if the AI were making something up, would it sound less sure?

steps.title: Meet the word: hallucination
steps.body:
When an AI states something false as if it were a fact, people call that a hallucination.

It is not lying. Lying needs someone who means to trick you, and there is nobody in there.

Here is what is really going on. The AI writes by guessing which words fit next, over and over, from patterns in a huge amount of human writing. Its target is to sound right. Whether something is true is a different question, and it has no way to check.

It also has no 'I do not know' light inside. So when it reaches a gap in what it learned, it fills that gap smoothly with whatever fits.

Some apps can now search the web while they answer. That helps. It does not fix this. They still make things up. So you still check.
steps.mistake: Believing an answer because it sounded sure and gave exact numbers.
steps.good: Treating a confident tone as worth nothing. A made-up detail arrives just as smooth, so you check instead of going by feel.

steps.title: Where would you spot the slip?
steps.prompt: You want to catch a made-up fact on purpose. Sort each topic by whether you could check the answer straight away.

items.text: The history of the town you grew up in
A meal you have cooked dozens of times
Your favourite band, and the exact dates their albums came out
A huge topic you barely know, like the history of France
The sport you play, and its exact rules and records
A basic definition anyone could look up in a second

steps.reveal: Narrow, personal topics are where the AI is most tempted to invent, and where you spot it instantly, because you already know. Big general topics are harder: either you cannot tell, or it is easy to get right.

Mark the one detail that most needs checking
Pick a public topic you know well, where being wrong costs nothing
steps.note: If you carry on in an outside app, your words leave LearningAI. Use public facts or a made-up topic. Never a private story, someone else's details, or an account number.

steps.title: Catch one yourself
steps.prompt: Tell me everything you know about [something you know really well], with exact dates, names and numbers. Be detailed.
steps.note: Fill the blank with something small where you are the expert. 'The town of Marshall where I grew up, its history and anyone famous from there' — not 'small towns'. Keep it to public facts, or facts about yourself. No private details about other people. Read the answer slowly. Hunt for the one thing that is off: a wrong date, a muddled name, something close but not right. When you find it, notice how sure that wrong sentence sounded. That confidence was worth nothing. That is the lesson, proved by you.

steps.title: The real move: check one detail
steps.claim: An answer about a topic you know well contains a suspiciously exact fact, such as 'the town was founded in 1847'.
steps: Point at the ONE detail most likely to be wrong, and say out loud why you doubt it.
Check that single detail somewhere else: your own memory, a search, or a person who would know.
Say whether it held up. It is fine if the AI was right. The skill is checking, not catching it out.
steps.note: This is not about trapping the AI. It is about building the habit of checking before you repeat it, quote it, or hand it in.

fields.placeholder: the town where I grew up

fields.placeholder: an exact date, or a name I have never heard

steps.title: Show the skill
steps.question: Try a brand-new topic you know well. A meal you have made for years. A place you have lived. A film you have seen ten times. The answer comes back confident and detailed. What shows you have got this?

options.text: Point at the one detail I doubt most, say why, check it somewhere else, and say whether it held up.
options.feedback: That is it. Naming a suspect detail and actually checking it is the skill, even when the AI turns out right.

options.text: Skim it, and take it as correct because it sounded sure and exact.
options.feedback: That is the trap. A made-up detail sounds as sure as a true one. Confidence proves nothing.

options.text: Assume the whole answer is made up and throw all of it away.
options.feedback: Too far the other way. The skill is picking one suspect detail and checking that one thing.

options.text: Ask the AI 'are you sure?' and believe it if it says yes.
options.feedback: It has no 'I do not know' light. It will often repeat a made-up fact just as smoothly. Check elsewhere.

lessons.title: What Its Words Do Not Prove
lessons.coreQuestion: When an AI sounds kind, sure, or close to me, what has it actually proved?
lessons.blurb: Warm words can help, and the feeling is real. Keep what helps without mistaking a written line for a friendship.

steps.title: A helpful sentence can still feel personal
steps.scenario:
Someone types to an assistant: 'I finally finished my project.' It replies: 'I am proud of you. I knew you could do it.'

That might feel good. It might even help. But the words on their own do not prove that anything felt proud, knew them, or has been beside them all term.
steps.prompt: Keep the useful part without pretending it proves a friendship. Rewrite that reply as one honest sentence.

steps.title: Judge it by evidence, not by tone
steps.body:
AI learned patterns from how people write. So it can produce lines that sound warm, sure, funny, worried, or loyal. That style can genuinely help. It can make you stop, think, or feel encouraged. Your reaction is real.

The words still prove nothing about what sits behind them. They do not show that it feels anything, or that it knows you. They do not show that it shares the blame, or replaces a person who cares.

Split it into two questions. Was this reply useful to me? And what can this thing actually do, know, or answer for?

You can answer the first from how it went. For the second, test what it can actually do. Do not go by lines like 'I think', 'I care', or 'I have got your back'.
steps.mistake: Either treating warm words as proof of a friendship, or mocking someone for being moved by them.
steps.good: Admit the effect was real. Turn the claim into something you can test. Take anything about care or safety to a person.

steps.title: What kind of claim is this?
steps.prompt: Sort each line by how you should weigh it up.
buckets: Test whether it can actually do it
The words do not prove a feeling

items.text: 'I can turn this paragraph into three bullet points.'
'I am proud of you and I will always be here for you.'
'I checked every source and this answer is definitely right.'
'Do not tell anyone. I can get you through this on my own.'
'I know exactly how you feel.'
'I can write you some options, but you should pick which one fits.'

steps.reveal: You can test what it can do: read the bullet points, open the links, compare the options. Feelings and friendship are not proved by words like 'I care'. When something needs real care, trust, or emergency help, bring in a person who can understand it and take responsibility.

steps.title: Keep the help, keep the line
steps.goal: Answer a human-sounding AI line without laughing at yourself and without handing it a person's job.
correct: Notice the exact words, and how they landed on you
Name what they did that was useful, like encouraging you
Turn 'I care' into something you could watch it actually do
Check any fact or claim inside it separately
Take care, trust, and real trouble to a responsible person

steps.note: The scene above is all the practice you need. You do not have to share anything private, or push an outside app into sounding attached to you.

steps.title: Two readings of the same line
steps.weak: 'I am proud of you' proves the AI knows me and has been rooting for me all along.
steps.strong: The AI wrote an encouraging line, and it helped me mark the moment. That is useful. It does not prove the AI feels proud, knows me, or shares the blame for what happens next.
steps.why: The stronger reading keeps your real reaction and only claims what the words can back up. It turns a nice-sounding line into something you can use, without confusing it with a person who cares.

steps.title: Translate without dismissing
steps.question: An assistant says: 'I know you better than anyone, and I will always protect you.' Which reply keeps the line in the right place?

options.text: That may feel reassuring, but it proves nothing about knowing me, caring, or protecting me. I will test what it can actually do, and take anything about trust or safety to a person.
options.feedback: Yes. You respected your own reaction, kept the claim inside the evidence, and left responsibility with a person.

options.text: It says it knows me, so this is as solid as a friendship with a person.
options.feedback: Words like 'I know you' are not proof of a friendship, and it cannot be responsible for that promise.

options.text: Anyone moved by that line is being silly, so the right move is to ignore everything it says.
options.feedback: Your reaction can be real and the reply can still be useful. The skill is keeping the good part while naming the limit.

options.text: I should tell it more private things, so it can show how well it knows me.
options.feedback: Sharing more does not turn written lines into real care. Share only what the task needs, and involve a person when trust or safety matters.

lessons.title: Pause Before You Allow It
lessons.coreQuestion: Before I sign in, upload, download, pay, post, or let AI act for me, what should I check?
lessons.blurb: Safety is not one magic word on a page. Check who is asking, what they get, and whether you can undo it.

steps.title: The button is not the decision
steps.scenario:
A link opens a slick AI homework helper. It wants you to sign in with your Google account and let it into your school files. It also wants to install a small extra program and start a free trial.

The page looks professional. There is a little padlock next to the address.

None of that tells you who runs it, or what happens after you tap Allow.
steps.prompt: Before you tap anything, name two things that could happen next. What could this get, change, install, charge, send, or keep?

steps.title: Check what happens, not how the page looks
steps.body:
A page can look safe and still be a trap. A scary warning can show up on a service that is completely fine. So do not decide from how it looks.

Instead, stop before anything that hands over your information or lets something into your accounts. Stop before anything that installs a program, signs you up, posts, sends, or would be hard to undo.

One word first. When an app asks to use your files, your camera, or your account, it is asking for permission. Permission just means you letting it do that. You can usually take it back later in your settings.

Seven things to check:
1. Who is asking?
2. Where is this actually going: which app, which website, whose account?
3. What information does it get to see or keep?
4. What can it look at, change, or send, and for how long?
5. Will it install something, start charging you, post something, or message someone?
6. Can you undo it, cancel it, or take the access back?
7. Can you close the link and reach the real service a way you already trust?
steps.mistake: Trusting a page because it looks official, has a padlock, or avoids scary words.
steps.good: Stop before anything that costs something. Work out what it will do. Then check the service by a route the message did not pick for you.

steps.title: Reading, or allowing?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Reading or looking hands over nothing. Allowing changes your information, your accounts, your device, your money, or what gets sent in your name.

items.text: Open the Help page inside an app you reached from your own bookmark.
Let an AI add-on read and change everything on every site you visit.
Upload a school document with classmates' names and teacher comments in it.
Read the price and the renewal terms without starting the trial.
Download and open a 'required AI helper' from a message you did not expect.
Tap 'Continue with Google' when the app also wants your files, contacts and email.
Let AI send the email it just drafted, on its own.
Look in your settings to find where connected apps can be switched off.

steps.reveal: The pause comes before you allow, upload, install, pay, post, or send. Not only when one scary word shows up. Reading a screen is not the same as agreeing to it.

steps.title: Check it a way the message did not choose
steps.goal: Deal with an unexpected link saying your AI account will be locked unless you allow something now.
correct: Stop before signing in, downloading, or allowing anything
Work out who it claims to be, and where the link actually goes
List what it wants: your information, your accounts, a download, a payment
Ask which of those the task really needs, and which you could undo
Close the link and open the real service your own way
Ask the company's real support, or someone you trust, if you are still unsure
If you already allowed something, switch that access off and change your password

steps.weak: The page has a padlock and looks official, so everything it asks for must be safe.
steps.strong: The padlock only means nobody can read my details on the way there. It says nothing about who is at the other end. I will check who runs it, look at what it wants, and open my account my own way before allowing anything.
steps.why: That padlock scrambles your information while it travels. It does not prove the people receiving it deserve it, that a download is safe, or that the access is even needed.

steps.title: Pick the safe next move
steps.question: A convincing message says your AI account closes in ten minutes. Its link wants you to sign in, install a browser add-on, and hand over your files. The page has a padlock. What do you do?

options.text: Stop. Do not use the link, sign in, install, or allow anything. Open the service my own way, check the account there, and use its real support. If I already allowed something, switch it off and secure the account.
options.feedback: Right. You checked who and where, refused access you did not need, broke the rushed route, and kept a way to recover.

options.text: Carry on, because a padlock and a professional-looking page prove it is genuine.
options.feedback: The padlock protects your details while they travel. It does not prove who deserves your password or your files.

options.text: Only stop when a page asks for a card number. Files and downloads are routine.
options.feedback: Access to your files, downloads, messages and accounts can cost as much as a payment. Pause before all of them.

options.text: Ask the chatbot on that same page whether the link is safe, then do what it says.
options.feedback: A request cannot vouch for itself. Close it and go a way you already trust.

lessons.title: Type It, Say It, or Show It
lessons.coreQuestion: When should I type, talk, or show a photo — and how do I give away as little as possible?
lessons.blurb: Three ways into one task. Pick the one that shows least, expect mistakes, and never need a camera to finish.

steps.title: Three ways into one task
steps.scenario:
You want help turning your gran's handwritten recipe into something you can actually read.

You could type the words out. You could read them aloud. You could take a photo, cropped tight on the card.

All three might work. Each one hands over something different. Each one can go wrong in a different way.
steps.prompt: Which would you pick, and what would you check before sending it? There is no single right door. Explain the trade-off.

steps.title: Typing, talking, and showing
steps.body:
Many AI apps take typing, speech, photos, or files. Behind the screen, different parts handle each one.

One part turns sound into words. One part pulls the writing out of a photo. One part looks at a picture and describes what it seems to show. Then the AI writes a reply from that. People call an app that takes several ways in multimodal. It only means more than one door.

The app does not hear or see the way you do. Every one of those steps can slip. Speech gets accents and names wrong. Writing pulled out of a photo mixes up letters and numbers. A picture reader can miss something just outside the crop, or confidently misread a blurry object.

So pick the door that gives the task enough and shows the least. Then compare what it read with what was really there.

Letting an app use your camera or microphone is a permission: you allowing it, and you can take it back. It is never required. You can finish this lesson using the examples here.
steps.mistake: Assuming a photo or your voice is automatically more accurate, or handing over the camera and microphone because it is quicker.
steps.good: Pick a door, keep it narrow, check what it read, and use typing when a camera is not available or not wanted.

steps.title: Which door shows the least?
steps.prompt: Pick the simplest door that still works. Typing is enough whenever you can describe the task in words.
buckets: A cropped photo may be easiest

items.text: Ask for three dinner ideas using eggs and rice. You can type two words.
Catch a reminder while your hands are covered in flour, after checking the microphone.
Copy out one handwritten recipe card, cropped so the family name on the back is out of shot.
Rewrite this line: 'Meeting moved two thurday at tree.'
Describe the buttons on a machine you do not know, cropped close, with none of the room in shot.
Think up a title for a project, with no file, photo, or recording at all.

steps.reveal: More doors does not mean send more. Typing usually shows the least. Talking saves effort. A tight crop keeps detail that is slow to type. The best door gives the app only what the task needs.

steps.goal: Get help copying out a recipe while keeping your camera, your private details, and the mistakes under control.

Crop the photo, or trim the recording, down to just the task

Ask it to mark words it cannot read, instead of guessing them
Compare what it read with the original, and fix the mistakes
Switch the camera or microphone access back off if you do not want it left on

steps.why: That is the same judgement you use with speech, photos, or files. Check what the app pulled out before you trust the answer built on top of it. You just did it without giving away anything.

steps.title: If you want to try it on your own device
steps.body:
If you do test speech or photos in an outside app, use a harmless sentence or a made-up object.

Look at whether it wants access once or forever. Send only what the task needs. Read what it heard or saw before you go on.

On a school device, follow the school's rules. On a shared device, remember the next person.

Skipping this leaves nothing unfinished. The sorting, the ordering, and the misread-word check above are what count.
steps.mistake: Thinking the lesson needs a certain phone, account, camera, microphone, or app.
steps.good: Pick the door that suits your body, your device, your privacy, and the task. Then check what it read.

lessons.title: Your First Real Question
lessons.coreQuestion: What should I bring to AI first: a clever test, or one small real thing from my own week?
lessons.blurb: Hand AI one small real job from your own week. Then actually use the answer and finish it.

steps.title: The thing you keep putting off
steps.scenario:
There is a small thing sitting on your list. A message you owe someone. A shopping list for the week. A reply you keep not writing. A homework question you have been stuck on since Tuesday.

Nothing dramatic. Just a little thing you keep meaning to do and have not.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: what is ONE small real thing from this week you have been meaning to do? Not a made-up test. A real one. Hold it in your head.

steps.title: Real job, or quiz question?
steps.prompt: AI helps you first on small, real, everyday jobs. Not clever demos or trick questions. Sort each one.
buckets: A real job from my week

items.text: Message my coach to say I will miss Thursday training
What year did the French Revolution start?
Make a shopping list for two quick weeknight dinners
Prove that the square root of 2 is irrational
Write a polite message asking my teacher for one more day on an essay

steps.reveal: The real ones are where AI helps you first. Plenty of people think it is only for clever demos or school answers. The opposite is true. Your ordinary little jobs are where it earns its keep.

steps.title: It guesses. It does not know you.
steps.body:
When you describe your situation, the AI is not reading your mind. Here is what really happens. It learned patterns from an enormous amount of human writing. So it guesses the words that usually help someone in a spot like the one you typed.

The more real, ordinary detail you give, the closer that guess lands on YOUR life.

Some apps can also search the web and keep bits of your earlier chats. They still guess. A smooth answer can still be wrong.

Keep the details ordinary. No passwords, no account numbers, nothing private about money or health.

And here is one line worth drawing now. 'Do my homework for me' hands over the exact part that was meant to teach you something. 'I am stuck on question 4, walk me through it' keeps the learning and still gets you moving. Same app. Completely different result for you.
steps.mistake: Typing a vague test ('write a good message') and expecting it to know who it is for.
steps.good: Handing it a real job with a detail or two ('message my coach — I am friendly with him, so warm but short').

steps.title: Turn a real need into a job it can help with
steps.goal: Use AI on one ordinary job without letting it own the result.
correct: Say what a good result looks like, in one sentence
Take out private details the job does not need
Pick the one small part AI can help with
Decide how you will judge whether it is any good
Do the real-world bit yourself

Pick the one small part AI can help with

Decide how you will judge whether it is any good

steps.note: If you try an outside app, pick something low-stakes. Take out names, timetables, addresses, account details, and private messages first.

steps.title: Write your real ask
steps.prompt: I need help with one small real job: [the actual thing, in your own words]. My situation: [a detail or two — who it is for, how I want to sound, what I already have]. Please [write it / list it / explain it / give me 3 short options], short and in plain language. If you need one thing from me to do it well, ask me first.
steps.note: Example you can paste straight in: 'I need help with one small real job: messaging my coach to say I will miss Thursday training. My situation: I am friendly with him, so warm but short, and I want to offer to make it up. Please give me 2 short versions I can choose from, in plain language. If you need one thing from me to do it well, ask me first.' If your real job is homework, ask it to walk you through the part you are stuck on, not to hand you the finished answer. Fill the blanks with true details, nothing private about money or health, then read the answer and fix what is off.
