steps.question: You ran your ask on a brand-new real job, read the answer, and fixed what was off. What makes it a win?

options.text: One real thing in my week is actually done. I sent it, saved it, or took the step.
options.feedback: That is the whole skill. Using the answer for the real thing is the lesson, not a tidy answer sitting on a screen.

options.text: The AI wrote me a smooth, tidy answer, so I am finished.
options.feedback: Not yet. A smooth answer can still be wrong, and it was never the goal. The win is the thing getting done.

options.text: I asked it a hard quiz question and it got the answer right.
options.feedback: That is a demo, not your week. Bring a real job and actually use what comes back.

options.text: I copied its answer straight onto my homework without reading it.
options.feedback: That hands over the part that was meant to teach you. Ask it to walk you through where you are stuck instead.

lessons.title: How to Ask So It Actually Helps
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn a vague ask into one that gets a genuinely useful answer?
lessons.blurb: An ask is an instruction, not a wish. Add four things and watch the answer sharpen.

steps.title: The lazy one-liner
steps.scenario:
You open an AI app and type the first thing in your head: 'give me a study plan.'

It answers instantly. Seven days, no subject, nobody in particular.

It is fine. It is also useless to you.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: the AI did not fail. Given only 'give me a study plan', what did it have to work with? What could you have told it?

steps.title: An ask is an instruction, not a wish
steps.body:
Remember how it works. The AI guesses the words that fit next, from patterns in a huge amount of human writing.

What you type is called a prompt. It just means the words you give it to work from.

So the more you say about what you want, the fewer answers fit, and the closer it lands on you.

The fix is not a longer sentence. A long vague ask still gets a vague answer. Being specific is what helps, not being wordy.

Extra words earn their place only when they tell it something real. That means your goal, who you are, your limits, and the shape you want back.
steps.mistake: Padding a vague ask with more words: 'Please kindly provide a comprehensive and detailed study plan.' Still vague, just longer.
steps.good: Telling it something real: what you want to do, who you are, your limits, and how the answer should look.

steps.title: Which part is missing?
steps.prompt: Each line adds ONE real thing. Is it your Goal and Context — what you want to do, and who you are? Or your Constraints and Format — your limits, and the shape you want back?

items.text: 'Help me make a 5-day plan for my biology test.'
'I am 15, the test is Friday, and cell diagrams confuse me.'
'I get 45 minutes a night and no weekends.'
'Give it to me as a short table, one row per day.'
'Put one practice question in each day.'

steps.reveal: Goal is what you want to DO. Not 'tell me about X' but 'help me do Y'. Context is who you are, so the answer fits you and not a stranger. Constraints are your limits and must-haves: time, money, reading level, things to leave out. Format is the shape you want back: a list, a table, three sentences, steps.

steps.title: Watch the gap open up
steps.weak: 'give me a study plan' -> a bland week-long plan, no subject, nobody in particular.
steps.strong: 'Goal: help me make a 5-day plan for my biology test. Context: I am 15, the test is Friday, cell diagrams confuse me. Constraints: 45 minutes a night, no weekends, one practice question a day. Format: a short table, one row per day.' -> a plan built around cell diagrams, cut to 45 minutes, with a question every day.
steps.why: Same AI. The strong one just narrowed what could fit. Every part you added threw away a cloud of answers meant for somebody else.

steps.title: Repair a vague ask without oversharing
steps.weak: Make this better. Here is the whole private chat and everyone's names.
steps.strong: Help me [what I want to do]. The background you need is [the background it needs]. Stick to these limits: [my limits]. Give it back as [the shape I want back]. Do not invent facts you do not have. Ask me one question if you need to.

steps.title: If you test it outside, send only what the job needs
steps.body:
If you take your repaired ask into an outside app, those words leave LearningAI. Swap real names, your school, account details, health information, exact addresses, and private messages for made-up stand-ins.

The repair above is what counts. Going outside is optional.

One more thing, about homework. Asking it to write your essay hands over the part that was supposed to teach you. Asking it to explain the step you are stuck on does not. You decide which of those you are asking for, and your Goal is where you say it.
steps.mistake: Adding sensitive detail because more background sounds automatically better.
steps.good: Add background that matters. Do not add yourself.

steps.title: Rebuild your own, one part at a time
steps.prompt: Goal: [what you want to do]. Context: [who you are and your situation]. Constraints: [your limits and must-haves]. Format: [the shape you want back]. Write the answer, then tell me in one line which part of my ask shaped it most.
steps.note: Add the parts one at a time and run it again after each. Goal, run. Add Context, run. Add Constraints, run. Add Format, run. Running again is cheap, because the chat still holds everything you said. Put your first answer and your last one side by side. That gap is the whole lesson. Only share background that matters, and no private details you do not need to hand over.

fields.label: Goal — what I want to do
fields.placeholder: help me make a 5-day plan for my biology test

fields.label: Context — who I am
fields.placeholder: I am 15, the test is Friday, cell diagrams confuse me

fields.label: Constraints — my limits
fields.placeholder: 45 min a night, no weekends, one question a day

fields.label: Format — the shape I want back
fields.placeholder: a short table, one row per day: topic, what to do, question

steps.title: You have got it when...
steps.question: Take a fresh weak ask you have not touched today: 'help me plan a birthday party', or 'write a message to my form tutor'. Add the four parts one at a time, running it again each time. What shows you actually get it?

options.text: You can point at the single part that made the biggest difference for THAT ask, and say why.
options.feedback: Yes. The win is not memorising four words. It is knowing what each one is for, and seeing which did the heavy lifting here.

options.text: You wrote the longest, most detailed ask you could.
options.feedback: Length is not the point. A long vague ask still gets a vague answer. Specific beats wordy every time.

options.text: You got a good answer first try without changing anything.
options.feedback: Maybe you got lucky. The skill is steering. If you cannot name what shaped the answer, you cannot repeat it.

options.text: You used the four words Goal, Context, Constraints, Format as headings.
options.feedback: The labels are only scaffolding. What matters is that you put something real under each one.

lessons.title: Fix It With One Reply
lessons.coreQuestion: When an answer is almost right, how do I fix it with one short reply instead of starting again?
lessons.blurb: Nudge a nearly-right answer with one line. No deleting, no retyping.

steps.title: The answer that is almost right
steps.scenario:
You asked for a thank-you message for your aunt. What came back is six stiff sentences. Too long, too formal, nothing like how you talk.

It is close. It is just not quite it.
steps.prompt: Before you read on, what is your first instinct? Delete it and write a better question? Or reply and fix the one you have?

steps.title: The second message is the steering wheel
steps.body:
Here is what is really going on. Inside one chat, the AI can see everything said so far. Your question, its answer, and now your reply.

So a short line like 'shorter, please' arrives as 'redo that last thing, but shorter'.

People say the AI remembers. That is a comparison, not the truth. Your earlier messages are simply still sitting in front of it while it guesses the next ones.

Start a brand-new chat and it can see none of that. You would have to build the whole request again from scratch.

That is why one line is enough to steer.
steps.mistake: Scrapping a close answer and retyping the whole question, throwing away the part that already worked.
steps.good: Sending ONE reply that keeps the good parts and changes only what is off.

steps.title: Retype it, or nudge it
steps.weak: Delete the answer, then retype everything: 'Write me a warm, friendly thank-you message, four sentences, mentioning the dinner, not too formal, that sounds like me...'
steps.strong: Just reply: 'That is close, but it is too long and too formal. Keep the rest the same. Cut it to four sentences and make it friendlier.'
steps.why: The nudge is a fraction of the typing and it keeps everything you already liked. The AI can still see its own answer, so 'keep the rest the same' has something real to hold onto.

steps.title: One change at a time
steps.prompt: You want to steer an answer without losing what worked. Sort each reply by whether it changes ONE clear thing or piles on several.

items.text: Make it shorter — about four sentences.
Make it warmer.
Make it shorter, warmer, add a joke, and change the ending.
Drop the last paragraph.
Rewrite the whole thing completely differently.

steps.reveal: Change ONE thing per reply. Then you can see exactly what each nudge did. If you do not like the result, you know which reply to undo. Five changes at once hide which one mattered.

steps.title: Change one thing and keep the result visible
steps.goal: Improve a message without losing your voice or changing five things at once.
correct: Name the one part that is not working
Protect the parts that already fit
Ask for one change you could point at
Compare the new version with what you actually wanted
Rewrite it and approve the final message yourself
choices: Protect the parts that already fit
Rewrite it and approve the final message yourself
Name the one part that is not working
Compare the new version with what you actually wanted
Ask for one change you could point at
steps.note: If you test a follow-up outside LearningAI, use a made-up draft, or take out names, private messages, and account details first.

steps.title: Send one nudge
steps.prompt: That is close, but [what is off about it]. Keep the rest the same and just [the one change you want].
steps.note: Fill the blanks with the single biggest problem and the exact fix. Example: 'That is close, but it is too long and too formal. Keep the rest the same and just cut it to four sentences and make it friendlier.' Watch it adjust the same answer in place. Still off? Nudge again — 'now add a line about the dinner' — without ever retyping the original question. This works on homework help too: 'that explanation lost me at step 3, explain just that step with an example'.

fields.label: My length nudge
fields.placeholder: shorter — about four sentences

fields.label: My tone nudge
fields.placeholder: warmer, or less like a textbook

fields.label: My trim nudge
fields.placeholder: drop the last part, keep the rest the same

steps.title: Did you steer it with replies alone?
steps.question: Take a fresh answer you did not like. A new question, not the thank-you message. Improve it using replies only, with nothing retyped. When it comes good, which is true?

options.text: I fixed it with replies alone, and I can name the one nudge that did the work.
options.feedback: That is the skill. You steered the answer you already had, and you know which nudge mattered.

options.text: I deleted it and wrote a stronger question from scratch.
options.feedback: That is starting over. It works, but it throws away the good parts, and it is not the skill here. Try again with replies only.

options.text: I sent one reply changing five things, and I cannot tell which one fixed it.
options.feedback: Change one thing per reply. Otherwise you cannot see which nudge worked, or undo the one that did not.

lessons.title: The One Privacy Rule
lessons.coreQuestion: What is the one question to ask before you send, and what should you take out first?
lessons.blurb: Before you send, ask: would I be fine if this were public? Then scrub whatever you would not.

steps.title: A postcard, not a diary
steps.scenario:
You want help sorting out a charge nobody in your family recognises. You start typing the full card number, the name of the shop worker, and your home address.

It feels private. Just you and a chat box.

But those details leave LearningAI and land in another company's system. And the writing job did not need a single one of them.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: which parts of that message would you not want a stranger to read? Name them.

steps.title: Safe, or never share?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Safe to type into an AI, or on the never-share list? Never-share means passwords and logins, full ID or bank or account numbers, or another person's full name plus their private business.

items.text: 'There is a charge for about $300 that nobody recognises.'
'Help me write a polite email to the bank.'
My password (even though the message said it was urgent)
'My neighbour Dan Reyes, 14 Oak St, is behind on his medical bills.'
'Someone in my family is having a hard time and I want to help.'

steps.reveal: The rough amount and the request are enough on their own. The account number, the password, the address, and another person's details were never needed. No urgent-sounding message changes that.

steps.title: The one public test
steps.body:
The mistake: 'It is a private chat box, so what I type stays between me and the AI.'

Not quite. What you type goes to the company running it. What happens after that depends on the app, your account, your settings, and their current rules. It might be kept for a while. People there may be allowed to read some of it. It may be used to improve the system. It may come back later through a memory feature. None of those is true of every app, so check the settings and the rules of the one you actually use.

One rule survives all of that. Before you send, ask: would I be fine if this turned up somewhere public? Then take out anything you would not.

Some details do more damage than they look. Your home address and school name together tell a stranger where to find you most days. Swap both for something general.

An AI is a tool. It is not a friend, a counsellor, or someone who can be responsible for you. For anything serious, bring in a real person or a professional you trust.
steps.mistake: Pasting your real message with the card number, the password, and a neighbour's address still in it. All because the box feels private.
steps.good: You decide what leaves your device. Run the public test, then take out every password, full number, and other person's private detail before you send.

steps.title: Blur it before you send
steps.weak: Help me write a polite email about a wrong charge of $312 on [full card number] to [a real person's name], who lives at [home address].
steps.strong: Help me write a polite email about a wrong charge on [my card] for [the amount] to [the shop].

steps.title: Run the privacy scan yourself
steps.goal: Turn a made-up message into one that is safe to send, without relying on another AI to spot the risk.
correct: Circle every real name, exact place, school, workplace, account detail, password, private message, photo, and fact about another person
Delete anything the job does not need
Swap what is left for stand-ins like [a relative], [the amount], or [my card]
Read it back as if it were public, and ask what a stranger could work out
If it could still cause harm or embarrassment, do not send it. Ask a trusted person or a professional instead
steps.note: This scan on its own finishes the activity. No outside app is needed, and none of them should ever be your final judge of what is private.

fields.label: What I take out before sending
fields.placeholder: Names, passwords, places, full numbers, private messages

fields.label: Stand-ins I can use instead
fields.placeholder: [a relative], [the amount], [my card]

steps.title: Scrub a brand-new message
steps.question: Take a different message you have not scrubbed yet. Which final version means you have the skill?

options.text: One a stranger could read and learn nothing they could use against me or anyone else. Every private part named, sorted, and swapped for a stand-in.
options.feedback: Exactly. Name each private part, know which kind it is, blur it, and check that a stranger would learn nothing usable.

options.text: One where I left the real details in, because the chat feels private and it is faster.
options.feedback: It only feels private. Your words leave your device, and what happens next depends on the app and its settings. Scrub first.

options.text: One where I took out my own card number but kept a neighbour's full name and home address.
options.feedback: Other people's details count too. A full name plus their address, health, money, or secrets is not yours to hand over.

lessons.title: Who Is in Charge
lessons.coreQuestion: If the AI writes it, who is actually in charge, and which part is still my job?
lessons.blurb: AI can do the middle of a job. You keep the goal, the way you want it, and the last look.

steps.title: It wrote the whole thing. So who decided?
steps.scenario:
Your gran sent you money for your birthday. You ask an AI app to write the thank-you message.

Five seconds later it is there. Neat, polite, finished. You nearly send it.

Then you read the first line. 'Dear valued family member.' You have never said that in your life.
steps.prompt: The AI typed every word. Does that mean it was in charge? Which part of that job was never its to decide?

steps.title: It does the middle. You hold both ends.
steps.body:
The AI wrote every word and still decided nothing. Here is what it actually does.

It has read an enormous amount of human writing. When you type something, it guesses which words usually come next. Then the next. Then the next. That is the whole trick.

Some apps can also search the web, or keep bits of your older chats. They are still guessing.

So it can fill in the middle of a job. It cannot want anything. It has no idea what counts as good to you.

Three jobs stay yours.

The goal. What you actually want.

The way. How you want it done.

The last look. You reading it and saying yes before you use it.

Letting it type for you is not the same as letting it decide for you.
steps.mistake: Handing over the whole thing — 'write my thank-you message' — and sending back whatever turns up.
steps.good: Handing over only the middle. You say the goal and the way. It drafts. You check it before it goes anywhere.

steps.title: Whose job is it?
steps.prompt: Sort each piece of the job. AI can handle the busy middle. Three things stay with you.

items.text: Deciding it should sound warm and like me, not stiff
Writing a first draft in five seconds
Choosing that it stays under four sentences and mentions the money
Looking up a nicer way to word one awkward line
Reading it against what I wanted and saying yes before I send it

steps.reveal: The drafting and the looking-up are the middle. AI is happy to do those. The goal (warm, like me), the way (short, mention the money), and the last look never left you. Those are the two ends you hold.

steps.title: Mark where the job changes hands
steps.goal: Use AI to help make a poster for the school charity match, without letting it make the calls that matter.
correct: You decide who the poster is for and what it has to do
You take out phone numbers and anything private a poster does not need
AI writes a few different layouts to choose from
You check the date, the rules, and how people get in
You pick one, fix what is off, and say yes before it goes up
choices: You check the date, the rules, and how people get in
AI writes a few different layouts to choose from
You pick one, fix what is off, and say yes before it goes up
You take out phone numbers and anything private a poster does not need
You decide who the poster is for and what it has to do
steps.note: If an outside app writes the draft, your words leave LearningAI. Stick to facts a poster on a wall would show anyway. Do not paste lists of names, phone numbers, or private messages.

steps.title: Run one real job and keep the three parts
steps.prompt:
Pick one small real thing you have to do today. Write three lines first: 'My goal is ___.' 'The way I want it is ___.' 'I will check it by ___.' THEN send this:

"Help me with the middle of this. Do not decide it for me: [the job]. My goal is [goal]. I want it done this way: [the way]. Give me a draft I can read, then list 2 or 3 things I should double-check before I trust it."
steps.note: Example fill-ins — job: 'write a short thank-you message to my gran for the birthday money.' goal: 'it sounds warm and like me, not stiff.' way: 'under four sentences, and mention what I am saving up for.' When the draft lands, read it out loud against your goal. Ask: is this what I actually wanted? The moment you feel like just sending it is the moment your check matters most. If the job is homework, ask it to walk you through the bit you are stuck on. Asking it to hand you the finished answer gives away the part that was meant to teach you.

fields.label: My goal
fields.placeholder: What done well means to me, in my own words

fields.label: The way I want it
fields.placeholder: How it should be done — under four sentences, mention the money

fields.label: I will check it by
fields.placeholder: How I test it before I trust it — read it against my goal, check each fact

steps.title: Show that you held the wheel
steps.question: Take a brand-new job of your own, not the thank-you message. Say all three lines before you type anything. Run it, then do your check. What proves you were in charge?

options.text: I can point at the spot where I caught something. A place the draft missed my goal or my way, and I changed it.
options.feedback: Yes. That caught-it moment is the proof. You held the goal, the way, and the last look, and let AI do only the middle.

options.text: The draft was so good I sent it without changing anything.
options.feedback: Sending it untouched means you skipped your check. It can sound sure of itself and still be wrong, or just not what you wanted.

options.text: I handed over the whole job and let the AI work out what good meant.
options.feedback: That gives away the goal, which is the one thing it must not decide. It has no idea what good means to you.

options.text: It finished so fast that there was nothing left to check.
options.feedback: Speed is not a check. Fast and confident is exactly when a made-up detail slips past you. Read it anyway.

lessons.title: Check It Before You Trust It
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I tell whether the source an AI gives me really backs up what it said?
lessons.blurb: A link proves nothing until you open it and find the fact sitting there on the page.

steps.title: The answer that looks airtight
steps.scenario:
You ask an AI app a question for your class presentation. The answer comes back sounding certain.

Underneath it lists where the fact came from. A title, a writer, a date, even a link that opens.

It looks solid. Your slide is nearly done.
steps.prompt: What has the AI actually proved by handing you that link? That the page is real? That the page says the thing it claimed?

steps.title: A source is decoration until you open it
steps.body:
A source is simply where a fact came from. A website, a book, a report by people who study that thing.

Here is the problem. The AI guesses words that fit the shape of a good answer. A tidy source name fits that shape perfectly. So it can hand you one that is out of date, is about something else, or was never real at all.

There is a second trap, and it catches more people. Plenty of apps really do search the web. They give you a genuine link that genuinely opens. That still proves nothing on its own. The page may simply not say what the AI said it says.

The link opening is not the test. The page saying the thing is the test.

Think of a receipt. Anyone can print one. You only believe it once you see the money actually gone from the account. That is a comparison, not the real thing. What is really happening is plainer: the AI wrote something shaped like a good source, and nothing checked it.
steps.mistake: It gave me a link and an author, so the answer must be backed up.
steps.good: I open it myself, see that it is real, and find the fact on the page before I trust it.

steps.title: Three checks, in this order
steps.goal: Turn one AI claim plus its source into a verdict you can defend
correct: Ask the AI for its single best source, and the exact sentence in it that backs the answer
Open it yourself — click the link, or search the title and the writer's name
Check 1 — Is it there? Does the link open, or does the title turn up at all?
Check 2 — Is it a real place: a known site, a proper study, a real organisation?
Check 3 — Does it actually say it? Can you find that exact fact on the page?
Give it one word: Checked, Does not match, or Not found
steps.note: A page that wants you to pay or log in is not proof it is fake. 'I cannot open it' is not the same as 'it does not exist.' Try another way in before you judge. If any of the three checks fails, the claim is not proven, and you just caught it in time.

steps.title: Judge a source trail
steps.claim: A local swimming pool lets anyone under 16 swim on their own after 6 p.m.
steps: Write down exactly what is being allowed, and who it affects
Go to the pool's own current rules, not to another AI answer
Check the place, the age rule, the date, and any exceptions
Write down one word: Checked, Does not match, or Not found
If it is still unclear, do not act until the pool or a responsible adult confirms it
steps.note: This trail is enough to practise on. It uses no real names, no real address, and nobody's actual timetable.

steps.title: If you go outside, keep the question clean
steps.body:
If you carry on in an outside app, your words leave LearningAI. Pick a public claim that does not matter much.

Do not share a real person's name, age, timetable, health detail, account number, or private message.

The source you open is what earns the verdict. Not the chatbot.
steps.mistake: Adding personal details to make a public fact easier to look up.
steps.good: Asking about the public claim only, then going and reading the source yourself.

steps.title: Ask for the source AND the exact sentence
steps.prompt: Answer this question: [question]. Then give me the single best source for it, the exact sentence from that source that backs it up, and a link, or the title, writer and date. Keep it to [number] source(s). I am going to open it and check that it really says this, so do not invent anything. If you are not sure a real source exists, say so instead.
steps.note: For [question], pick one specific fact that should have a real, findable source. Something like: how much water should an adult drink in a day, and who says so? For [number], start with one. Use two if you want a second opinion. Then actually open it and run the three checks.

fields.label: The claim I am checking
fields.placeholder: Adults should drink 8 cups of water a day

fields.label: The source it gave me
fields.placeholder: A link, or a title, writer and date

fields.label: The sentence that should prove it
fields.placeholder: Paste the sentence the AI quoted

fields.label: My verdict after opening it
fields.placeholder: Checked / Does not match / Not found — and the sentence that earns it

steps.title: Earn a verdict on a claim of your own
steps.question: Pick a brand-new question of your own, not the water one. Run the prompt and open the source. What counts as doing this well?

options.text: The AI wrote 'verified', so I am done. Getting that word back is the goal.
options.feedback: The AI's own word is not the check. The win is you reaching a verdict by opening the source, whatever that verdict turns out to be.

options.text: I opened the source and ran the three checks. Then I wrote one word: Checked, Does not match, or Not found. I can point at the exact sentence that earns it, or at the fact it is missing.
options.feedback: That is it. Reaching a verdict you can defend on a fresh claim is the win, not collecting a tick.

options.text: The link opened and the page looked professional, so I trusted the claim without reading it.
options.feedback: That is the modern trap. A working link proves the page exists. Check 3 is the one that matters.

options.text: The page wanted me to pay, so I marked the claim as made up.
options.feedback: A paywall is not proof of anything. 'I cannot open it' is not 'it does not exist.' Try another way in first.

lessons.title: AI Is Already in Your Apps
lessons.coreQuestion: Where is AI quietly shaping what an app shows me, and what should change how much I trust it?
lessons.blurb: Spot the quiet AI bits in apps you already use. Read what the app itself says they do. Check harder when a mistake would cost you.

steps.title: Nothing announced itself
steps.scenario:
Your photo app has quietly gathered every picture of your best friend into one folder. Your email offers you a ready-made reply. A search page writes you a paragraph before any of the links.

None of them said 'this is AI'. Each one is doing a different job, and the same app can behave differently on a school account.
steps.prompt: Before you rely on one of these, which matters more: whether the word AI appears anywhere, or what happens if it gets it wrong?

steps.title: Look at the evidence, not the buzzword
steps.prompt: Sort each clue by what it can honestly tell you. These are all built in, so you do not need any particular phone.
buckets: Tells me something real about this feature

items.text: The app's own help page says photo search matches faces, and shows how to fix a wrong match.
A chatbot says the feature 'probably uses AI somewhere'.
A setting names the feature, shows whether it is on, and says what it is allowed to look at.
The answer arrived fast and looked futuristic.
Your school says this feature is switched off on school accounts.
A friend has the same app and assumes every account works the same.

steps.reveal: A label, a slick animation, or a confident guess tells you nothing about how one feature works. The app's own help page, the settings you can see, and your school's rules are far stronger. Even then, stay on the choice in front of you. What does the feature do? What can it see? What would a mistake cost?

steps.title: Lots of different jobs, not one hidden brain
steps.body:
AI inside everyday apps is not one recipe copied everywhere. Different parts do different jobs.

One puts search results in an order. One matches pictures to each other. One turns speech into text. One writes new sentences or makes new images.

Plenty of features mix a guessing part with plain fixed rules, or with a person checking the result.

You do not have to name every piece before you use something. You need enough to answer four questions.

What job is this feature doing?

What is it allowed to see?

Can I turn it off, correct it, or undo a mistake?

What changes if it gets it wrong?
steps.mistake: Treating 'AI' as one yes-or-no label, then trusting or refusing every feature the same way.
steps.good: Looking at the actual feature and its settings, then checking harder as the cost of a mistake goes up.

steps.title: Look before you lean on it
steps.goal: A calendar app suggests a time for your study group. Get it wrong and somebody turns up to an empty room. Put the check in order.
correct: Name the thing you might rely on: the time it suggested
Read the app's own label, help page, settings, or your school's rules, instead of asking another AI to guess
Check what it looked at, and whether you can correct the suggestion or switch it off
Compare the suggestion with the real calendar entry, because getting it wrong costs somebody an afternoon
If it is wrong, fix the entry, then change or switch off the feature before next time
choices: Compare the suggestion with the real calendar entry, because getting it wrong costs somebody an afternoon
Name the thing you might rely on: the time it suggested
If it is wrong, fix the entry, then change or switch off the feature before next time
Check what it looked at, and whether you can correct the suggestion or switch it off
Read the app's own label, help page, settings, or your school's rules, instead of asking another AI to guess
steps.note: If a mistake costs nothing, this takes seconds. For health, money, school, work, safety, or somebody else's private information, slow down and check a source that actually knows.

steps.title: Optional: look up one real feature
steps.prompt: Pick one ordinary feature you can safely look into. Or use this one: 'an email app offers a ready-made reply.' Find the app's own label, help text, or setting. Write down four things: what job it says it does, what control you have, one way it could be wrong, and how you would fix it if it were.
steps.note: You do not need to list your real apps or devices. Do not share account names, contacts, messages, photos, school details, or where you have been. If the app explains nothing, write 'not stated' rather than asking a chatbot to invent an explanation.

fields.label: The feature and its job
fields.placeholder: Calendar suggests a time for the study group

fields.label: What tells me how it works
fields.placeholder: The help page, a setting, or a school rule

fields.label: What a mistake would cost
fields.placeholder: Somebody turns up to an empty room

fields.label: How I fix it or switch it off
fields.placeholder: Compare with the invite, fix it, then turn suggestions off

steps.title: Pick the check that actually holds up
steps.question: A writing app quietly rewrites a sentence in a message to your teacher. Which response shows the whole skill?

options.text: I find the rewrite setting and read what it says it does. Then I reread the changed sentence, because this message matters, and undo it if the meaning shifted.
options.feedback: Yes. You used what you could actually see, checked harder because it mattered, and kept a way to undo it.

options.text: It looks like AI, so I decide it is unsafe and never open the app again.
options.feedback: The label alone does not settle it. Look at the feature, its settings, and what a mistake would cost.

options.text: I ask a different chatbot whether this app uses AI, and believe whatever it says.
options.feedback: That is one more guess. Use the app's own help page, the settings you can see, and any school rule.

options.text: Grammar changes are usually harmless, so I send it without rereading.
options.feedback: The cost depends on this message, not on the type of feature. A changed meaning going to a teacher is worth ten seconds.

lessons.title: A Daily Habit, Not a Crutch
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI every day so my own thinking gets sharper instead of switching off?
lessons.blurb: Use AI often, without handing over the part you wanted your own brain to learn.

steps.title: Two ways to use the same app
steps.scenario:
Your friend's mum has driven you to football three weekends running. You owe her a thank-you text.

You could type 'write a thank-you text' and send back whatever appears. Or you could write a rough one yourself, then ask AI to tighten it.

Same job. Same app. Same five minutes.
steps.prompt: After each of those, which one leaves something behind in your head? A sentence you shaped, a choice you made. Say it in one line.

steps.title: Crutch, or coach?
steps.prompt: Underneath, the AI is guessing likely next words either way. What changes is what you ask for. Sort each one: does it think for you, or does it make you think and then help?

items.text: "Write my whole essay on this book."
"I will write the reply first. Then show me two lines I could cut."
"Just give me the answer to this maths question."
"Ask me a question that shows whether I actually understood the chapter."
"Rewrite this so it sounds clever. I do not want to touch it."
"Wait for my attempt, then tell me one thing to fix next time."

steps.reveal: Same machine, different instructions. Crutch and coach are a comparison to help you feel the difference. They are not a claim about what is going on inside. These apps can search, take several steps, and sometimes keep bits of old chats. None of that lets them choose which of your own skills you want to protect. You draw that line.

steps.title: A good habit ends with your brain switched on
steps.body:
Using AI every day does not make you lazy on its own. It depends entirely on how you use it.

Here is what it does. It has read an enormous amount of human writing, and it guesses the words that usually come next. Ask it to do the job, and it does the job. Your brain stays off.

Ask it to make you try first and only then help, and it waits. Your brain stays on.

A good habit is one that leaves your thinking sharper afterwards, not switched off.

One more thing. AI is not a friend, and it is not a doctor or a counsellor. For anything about your health, your safety, or a hard personal decision, bring in a real person you trust.
steps.mistake: "Write this for me." You paste the result, learn nothing, and the skill never becomes yours.
steps.good: "I will do my part first, then you help." You keep one step for yourself, so the skill stays yours.

I want a 5-minute habit that makes me sharper at [an area, for example writing clear messages] instead of dependent on you. Don't do the work for me — make me try first, then coach me. The one step I will always do myself is: [your step]. Give me one small practice task, wait for my try, then point out one thing worth improving.

steps.question: Tomorrow, on a new real job, you run your habit and hold that one step for yourself. Afterwards, which sentence means you got it right?

options.text: "I wrote the whole message myself. AI trimmed two wordy lines, and I kept my own opening."
options.feedback: That is the win. You can name a specific thing you did that it did not. The skill stayed yours.

options.feedback: Picking is a real decision, but it is not practice at writing. If writing is the skill you want, make your own rough version first.

lessons.title: When It Seems to Remember
lessons.coreQuestion: When an AI seems to remember me, what is actually going on, and what can I really check?
lessons.blurb: Five different things all get called memory. Telling them apart stops an empty Memory screen from feeling like a promise.

steps.title: Forgotten here does not mean gone
steps.scenario:
You tell a chatbot one made-up thing: your houseplant is called Gerald.

Later in the same chat it mentions Gerald. You open a new chat and it has no idea who Gerald is. The old chat is still sitting in your list. The Memory screen is empty.
steps.prompt: What has that little test actually proved? And what have you learned nothing about yet?

steps.title: Five different things, one word
steps.body:
Apps use the word memory for five different things. Keeping them apart is the whole skill.

1. Still in this chat. Everything you typed in this conversation is sitting in front of it while it writes. That is why it can use something from ten messages ago.

2. Your chat list. The company keeps a copy of the conversation. Seeing an old chat does not mean you are seeing every record they kept.

3. Remembered on purpose. Some apps save a few facts about you and bring them back in new chats.

4. Kept behind the scenes. How long copies stay, who at the company is allowed to look at them, and what the delete button actually removes.

5. Used to build the next one. Whether your chats may later help train the next version.

A new chat forgetting Gerald proves one of those. An empty Memory screen proves one setting is off. Neither one tells you about copies, staff, school rules, or training.
steps.mistake: Reading 'it forgot in a new chat' or 'Memory is empty' as proof that nothing is stored anywhere.
steps.good: Check the settings you can see, the company's current rules, and for a school account, the school's rules. Then only type things you could live with being kept.

steps.title: Which one is it?
steps.prompt: Sort each example into the thing it really describes. Real apps mix these up and label them differently, so the point is to keep the five questions separate in your head.
buckets: Used to build the next one

items.text: It uses a detail from ten messages ago to answer you now.
Yesterday's conversation is still there when you open the app.
A setting saves how you like answers laid out, and uses it in future chats.
The rules explain how long deleted chats stay in copies, and when staff are allowed to read them.
A switch decides whether your conversations may help train the next version.
A school sets a different time limit on how long chats are stored than a personal account has.

steps.reveal: Each one answers a different question. What it can see right now. What copies exist. What comes back in a new chat. How long things stay and who may read them. Whether any of it trains the next version. One switch might touch several of these. Never assume it settles all five.

steps.title: Only claim what you can show
steps.goal: You want to know what really happens to a harmless chat after you delete it. Put the digging in order.

Open the setting that covers it and write down only what it actually says
Read the company's current rules on keeping, deleting, staff access, and training
On a school or work account, check that place's own rules as well
Write down what you now know, what you still do not, and set a rule for what you will never type in

steps.note: If there is no memory setting at all, that tells you one thing: there is nowhere to manage saved facts. It does not prove there is no chat record, no copy, no time limit, no staff access, and no training rule.

steps.prompt: Use only the made-up fact that your houseplant is called Gerald. Check whether it sticks inside one chat. Then look at where this app shows your chat list, any saved facts about you, any switch about training, and a link to its rules. For each screen, write one sentence on what it proves and one on what it does not.

steps.question: A school account hides your chats after 30 days and has no memory switch at all. What can you honestly say about your data?

options.text: Only that the chats stop showing after 30 days and there is no saved-facts switch. I still need the company's rules and the school's rules to know about copies, time limits, staff access, deleting, and training.
options.feedback: Exactly. You matched what you claimed to what you could actually see, and kept the five questions apart.

options.text: Every copy is wiped after 30 days, because I cannot see the chats any more.
options.feedback: Not being able to see something is not the same as it being gone. Copies and records can outlive what shows on your screen.

options.text: There is no memory switch, so the account cannot be keeping anything at all.
options.feedback: A missing switch tells you about one setting. It says nothing about records, time limits, staff access, or school rules.

options.feedback: You need both. The rules describe the service. The settings show what is switched on for this account.

lessons.title: It Said It Did It
lessons.coreQuestion: Did it guess some words, really use a helper, or take steps on its own? How would I know?
lessons.blurb: Look for proof of what actually ran, what it was allowed to touch, and who had to say yes before anything changed.

steps.title: A plan is not proof
steps.scenario:
You ask an assistant to find you cheap football boots. It replies: 'I checked three shops, found the best price, and ordered them.'

It even lists the steps in order. Very tidy.

But there is no order number. No message from the shop. No money gone. It may have written about doing all that without doing any of it.
steps.prompt: What would show you it really did those things, rather than just writing that it did?

steps.title: Three different things get muddled up
steps.body:
Here they are in plain words.

The guesser. It reads what you gave it and guesses words that fit. People call it a model. On its own it only produces text. It cannot touch anything in the real world.

A helper. A separate piece of software the app can call on. A web search, a calculator, your calendar, a file. People call it a tool. A helper can fetch real facts, and it can change real things.

Working through steps on its own. The app picks a next step and calls a helper. It reads what came back, then picks the step after that. It keeps going until it decides to stop. People call this an agent.

These are not three sealed boxes. Something working through steps uses a guesser and helpers. An ordinary chat app might quietly call one helper for one answer.

So do not argue about the label. Ask five things you can look at.

What did you give it?

Which helper actually ran?

What was it allowed to touch?

What changed in the real world?

Where did a person say yes, stop, or undo it?
steps.mistake: Calling any long answer an agent, or treating a link as proof that a live search really ran.
steps.good: Look for a record of what ran, what it could touch, and what changed. If the app shows none of that, say you cannot tell.

steps.title: What does the proof actually show?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Use 'cannot tell' whenever the answer does not show what happened behind it.

items.text: You asked why bread rises. You got a general explanation. Nothing shows a helper running.
The record says helpers were switched off for this reply. Only your question and its answer were logged.
The record shows: calculator, 1487 x 23, answer 34,201. The reply uses that exact number.
The record shows: look up today's buses, compare arrival times, ask you to approve, add the chosen trip to a draft plan. Nothing is booked.
It says 'I checked the live web' but shows no helper, no source, no time, and no result.
A weather answer arrives with a logged call to a weather service and the time it ran.
A seven-step plan for tidying your files. No record that any file was ever opened or moved.

steps.reveal: Length, confidence, and the words 'I did this' are not proof. A logged helper shows something outside really ran. A chain of steps with a stopping point shows it worked on its own. Plenty of real apps hide all of this, so 'cannot tell' is often the honest answer.

steps.title: Put the yes before the change
steps.goal: An app may compare public bus times and put a plan together. It must not buy anything, message anyone, or use where you have been. Put the safety line in order.
correct: Say the goal, and which public information it may use
List what is off limits: where you have been, your messages, buying, changing accounts, sharing
Let it gather and compare public bus times, showing its sources and every helper it used
Make it stop at a draft and ask you to check the route, the time, and what could go wrong
Only you decide whether to use the plan. Nothing real has to change for this practice

steps.note: The more it does by itself, the more places you should stop and check. A real change is anything outside the answer: sending, buying, deleting, posting, booking, moving money, editing an account, or handing over private information.

Write down what you gave it, which helper ran, what came back, what it did next, where it asked you, and whether anything real changed. If it shows you nothing, use the bus-route example above and mark this one 'cannot tell'.

options.text: A record of each step it took and what came back every time. Plus when it decided to stop, and the point where a person had to say yes before anything changed.
options.feedback: Yes. The record, the steps, the stopping point, and the place a person approves are what settle it. Not the word it used about itself.

options.feedback: Describing itself is still guessed text. Look for what ran, what it could touch, and what changed.

options.feedback: A hard job does not prove how it was done. A guesser can describe a process it never carried out.

lessons.title: Three Dials You Can Turn
lessons.coreQuestion: How do the hat, the reader, and the shape each move an answer, and why turn one at a time?
lessons.blurb: Three separate dials, not one. Turn each on purpose and watch the answer move.

steps.title: Same question, four answers
steps.scenario:
You ask an AI how to revise for a science test. Then you ask three more times in the same chat.

Once telling it to answer like a patient teacher. Once saying it is for someone who has never really revised before. Once asking for a numbered checklist.

Four replies. All different.
steps.prompt: Which of those three changes do you think moves the answer most? And are they even doing different jobs?

steps.title: Three dials, not one
steps.body:
Three things steer an answer, and each one moves a different part.

The hat. Who you ask it to sound like. 'Answer like a patient teacher.' This mostly changes the tone and what gets stressed.

The reader. Who the answer is for. 'Written for someone who has never revised before.' This changes how simple or advanced it gets.

The shape. How it sits on the page. 'As a numbered checklist.' This changes the layout.

Why any of this works: the AI has read an enormous amount of human writing, and it guesses what fits next. A teacher's words, a note for a beginner, and a numbered list are three different patterns in that writing. Naming one pulls the guess towards it.

When we say it 'pretends to be a teacher', that is a comparison. It is not becoming anyone. It is leaning towards the kind of writing a teacher usually produces.

One thing that never changes. For real questions about health, money, or the law, treat the answer as a starting point. Check with someone qualified before you act.
steps.mistake: Turning all three dials at once, so you cannot tell which one did the work.
steps.good: Turning one dial at a time, so you can see exactly what each one moves.

steps.title: Which dial is this?
steps.prompt: Each phrase turns one dial. Sort it by what it changes: the hat, the reader, or the shape.

items.text: answer like a strict examiner
as a numbered checklist
reply like a calm older sister
as a do and don't list
for someone who has never played the game before
give it to me as a short table
for someone fixing a bike with only the tools in the shed

steps.reveal: The hat changes the voice and what gets stressed. The reader changes how much it assumes you already know. The shape changes the layout. You can use all three together, but turn one at a time when you want to know what helped.

steps.title: The reader is its own dial
steps.weak: How do I revise for a science test?
steps.strong: How do I revise for a science test? Written for someone who has never really revised before.
steps.why: The hat and the shape did not move. Only the reader did. Watch the second answer slow down, explain its words, and stop assuming things. That is the reader dial working on its own.

steps.title: Use all three on purpose
steps.prompt: This optional step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Use a harmless or made-up question. Do not paste names, private messages, health details, account details, or anything about another person. Answer like a [hat], written for [reader], as a [shape]: [your question].
steps.note: Pick something low-stakes: explaining a game rule, comparing two ways to fix something, writing a made-up notice for an event. For real health, money, or legal questions, take the facts to someone qualified before you act.

options.text: The second reply is longer, so the change clearly worked.
options.feedback: Longer is not the test. Point at the specific difference your one change caused. You can only trust that if nothing else moved.

options.text: I changed all three at once and the answer looks completely different.
options.feedback: Changing all three hides which one did the work. Turn exactly one, so the difference belongs to it.

lessons.title: Limits That Actually Stick
lessons.coreQuestion: Why do some limits I set get ignored while others hold, and how do I make one stick?
lessons.blurb: "Keep it short" slides straight off. "Exactly 3 bullet points" holds, because you can count them.

steps.title: You asked for short. You got an essay.
steps.scenario:
You typed "keep it short" and pressed send.

Back came five thick paragraphs.

You did set a limit. It rolled straight over it.
steps.prompt: What is the difference between "keep it short" and "exactly 3 bullet points"? Which one do you think it will actually stick to?

steps.title: A limit you can count is a limit that holds
steps.body:
A limit is a rule you put on the answer. How long it is. What to leave out. What word not to use.

A countable limit is one you can check afterwards by counting or looking. 'Exactly 3 bullet points.' 'Do not use the word amazing.'

Here is why that matters. The AI guesses the words that usually come next. It is not keeping a tally as it goes, and it is not measuring length.

So 'keep it short' has nothing solid in it. There is nothing to aim at, and it slides off. 'Exactly 3 bullet points' gives it a clear target.

One catch. A number of items holds up better than an exact word count, because it still is not really counting.

Which is the whole point. The skill is not the asking. The skill is the checking. Count them yourself, every time.
steps.mistake: Writing 'keep it short' or 'be brief' and hoping. There is nothing there to check against.
steps.good: Writing 'exactly 3 bullet points' and 'do not use the word amazing', then counting the bullets and searching for the word yourself.

steps.title: Countable, or just a feeling?
steps.prompt: Sort each limit. Could you check it afterwards by counting or looking? Or is it too vague to grade?

items.text: Exactly 3 bullet points
Keep it brief
Do not use the word 'utilise'
Make it sound professional
Answer in one short paragraph
Do not get too technical

steps.reveal: Countable limits leave you something to count or search for afterwards. Vague ones — brief, professional, too technical — leave you nothing to grade. Those are the ones that quietly get ignored.

steps.title: Swap the feeling for something you can count
steps.weak: Give me a quick rundown on what to check when buying a second-hand bike. Keep it brief and do not make it too salesy.
steps.strong: Answer this in exactly 3 bullet points. Do not use the word 'amazing'. Question: What should I look for when buying a second-hand bike?

Do not paste private messages, names, account details, or anything about another person. Answer this in [a limit I can count]. Do not use the word [word to avoid]. Question: [your low-stakes question]
steps.note: Pick something ordinary: a second-hand bike checklist, a plan for making lunches for the week, a reminder for games night. Then count the result and search for the banned word. If it missed, say exactly what it broke, ask for one fix, and check again.

lessons.title: Show It, Don't Describe It
lessons.coreQuestion: Why does pasting one example of the style I want beat describing that style in words?
lessons.blurb: Pick one safe example of the style you want and paste it in. Then decide what still needs to sound like you.

steps.title: The listing that came out wrong
steps.scenario:
You are selling your old skateboard online. You ask an AI for a short, friendly, casual description.

Back comes something stiff. Technically friendly. Technically casual. Nothing like how you actually write.

You add more words: warm, fun, chatty. It still misses.
steps.prompt: If you cannot quite put the style you want into words, what could you show it instead?

steps.title: One example beats a paragraph of describing
steps.body:
One real example you can point at teaches it faster than a paragraph trying to describe the same thing.

Here is why, and it is not magic. The AI has read an enormous amount of human writing, and it guesses which words come next. When you paste an example, you hand it a fresh pattern to carry on. It picks up the tone, the rhythm and the shape of your sample, and keeps going in that direction.

People sometimes say it 'gets your taste'. That is a comparison, not the truth. What is really happening is simpler. It reads the style of your example and continues it. It does not know you the way a friend does.

Giving exactly one example like this has a name. People call it a one-shot prompt. It is one of the biggest wins a beginner can pick up.
steps.mistake: Piling on more words — warm, casual, friendly, fun, chatty — trying to pin the style down perfectly.
steps.good: Pasting one real thing written in the style you actually want, and saying: now make a new one that matches this.

steps.title: Words only, or one example
steps.weak: Prompt: 'Write a short, friendly, casual description for my old skateboard.' Result: could be any board on any site — 'This quality skateboard offers great performance and is ideal for riders of all levels.'
steps.strong: Prompt pastes a real example first — the listing that sold your bike in a day: 'Old bike, still solid. Rode it two years, brakes are new, sold as I outgrew it. Collection only.' — then asks for the skateboard version in that same style. Result: 'Old board, still solid. Rode it a year, wheels are new, selling as I got a bigger one. Collection only.'
steps.why: The example gave it a real pattern to carry on: short opener, honest detail, one line about why you are selling. Words alone gave it nothing to match.

steps.title: Turn a description into a show-it prompt
steps.weak: Write a fun, casual caption for the football team photo in a voice people actually like.

This optional step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Use an example you wrote yourself, or a made-up one. Do not paste a friend's private message, anyone's personal details, or a long chunk of somebody else's published writing. Here is my example:
[a short thing you wrote]
Now write [the new thing] with a similar tone, length and shape. Do not copy the phrases, and do not pretend to be a real person.
