lessons.title: Get It to Teach You
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to actually learn something, instead of getting an answer I forget by tomorrow?
lessons.blurb: Turn a wall of answer into a lesson in small steps, then prove it stuck by saying it back.

steps.title: You had the answer an hour ago
steps.scenario:
You asked an AI to explain how interest works when someone borrows money. It gave you a neat, correct paragraph. You nodded and closed the tab.

An hour later a friend asks you the same thing. You open your mouth and nothing comes out.

You had the answer. It never made it into your head.
steps.prompt: If you cannot explain it an hour later, did you learn it? Or did you just watch it go past?

steps.title: Answer dump, or learning?
steps.prompt: Two things look identical on screen and land completely differently. An answer dump is the whole finished result handed to you in one block. Learning is when the idea ends up in your head, so you can say it back later. Sort each moment.

items.text: AI writes three tidy paragraphs. You copy them and move on.
AI teaches one small step, then stops to check you followed it.
You read a perfect explanation and cannot repeat it an hour later.
You say the whole idea back in your own words, without looking.
You got the right answer fast, so you assume you learned it.

steps.reveal: Fast and correct is not the same as understood. Having the answer and understanding the answer are two different things. Only one of them is still there tomorrow.

steps.title: Make it teach you, then check you
steps.body:
Remember what it is doing. It has read an enormous amount of human writing, and it guesses the words that usually come next.

It has seen countless explanations. So it can walk you through an idea one small step at a time. It can also spot when your version sounds off.

It is natural to call that having a tutor. That comparison is useful. Here is what is really going on, though. It is not a person. It does not know you and it does not care whether you pass. It guesses helpful-sounding words, which means it can say something wrong with total confidence.

That is exactly why you say it back. You are not trusting it to pour knowledge into you. You are using it to find the bits that are still fuzzy in your own head. You stay the judge of whether the explanation is right.

This is also where the line sits. 'Do my homework for me' hands over the part that was meant to teach you. 'I am stuck on question 4, walk me through it' keeps the learning and still gets you moving.
steps.mistake: Ask for the answer, read it, feel finished. Then confuse 'I saw a good explanation' with 'I understand this'.
steps.good: Ask it to teach in small steps and stop after each one. Then say the whole thing back in your own words and let it flag the part you got wrong.

steps.title: Run the teaching loop
steps.prompt: This optional step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Pick a public, low-stakes topic. Do not paste private schoolwork, names, grades, account details, or anything about another person. I want to understand [topic], not just get an answer. Teach me one small step, then stop and wait for my reply. Carry on only after I have had a go. At the end, ask me to explain it back, point out one gap, and tell me how to check the important fact somewhere outside this chat.
steps.note: Good topics: a setting on your phone, a rule in a card game, how gears work on a bike, why bread rises, how interest works using made-up numbers. Explain it back without scrolling up. A correction from AI is not automatically true. If the fact matters, check it against instructions, a calculator, or a source that actually knows.

fields.label: What I want to actually understand
fields.placeholder: how interest grows on borrowed money, month by month

fields.label: Where I am starting from
fields.placeholder: total beginner — I know what borrowing is, nothing about interest

fields.label: The check that makes it stick
fields.placeholder: stop after each step, then say the whole thing back from memory

steps.title: Prove it on a brand-new topic
steps.question: Pick something you have not touched today. A setting on your phone, a rule in a card game, why bread rises. Run the teaching loop, then look away from the screen and say the finished idea back in your own words. What tells you it worked?

options.text: I said it back correctly from memory, either first go or after fixing the one bit it flagged.
options.feedback: That is the win. Saying it back without looking means the idea is in your head, not just on your screen.

options.text: The explanation on screen looked complete and correct, so I am done.
options.feedback: A perfect explanation on screen is still a dump. You pass when you can say it back without peeking.

options.text: I could not say it back without scrolling up to reread it.
options.feedback: That was a dump, not learning. Run the loop again. Saying it back is the part that makes it stick.

options.text: I got the answer really fast, so I definitely learned it.
options.feedback: Fast and correct is not the same as understood. Test it by explaining it tomorrow, from memory.

lessons.title: Make the Answer Checkable
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I ask for working I can actually look at, without pretending the AI can show me its private thoughts?
lessons.blurb: Ask for what it assumed, where the facts came from, and the sums it did. Then check one of them yourself.

steps.title: Just a verdict
steps.scenario:
You ask an AI which phone deal costs less over a year. It replies: 'Plan B is cheaper.'

No sums. No working. Just the verdict.

It sounds sure of itself. You have no idea how it got there, or whether it added anything up correctly.
steps.prompt: If that verdict is wrong, could you tell? What would it need to show you before you could check?

steps.title: Ask for an audit trail, not private thoughts
steps.body:
An audit trail just means the working, laid out where you can look at it.

Here is the catch. These apps may do things inside that nobody can see. A tidy explanation written afterwards is not a recording of that. It is more writing.

So do not ask it to prove itself by showing you what is going on inside. Ask for working you can check.

The facts it used. What it assumed. The sums it did. Where each fact came from. Anything it is unsure about. One quick way for you to test the result.

All of that can still be wrong. But now you have something to grab hold of.

Your goal is not to watch it think. Your goal is to make the answer open enough that you can decide whether to trust it.
steps.mistake: 'It gave a really detailed explanation, so it must be right.' Detail makes a mistake sound more convincing, not less.
steps.good: Ask for the working you can check. Then test the part that matters most, yourself.

steps.title: Open up the answer
steps.goal: Turn a bare verdict into a few claims you can look at, then actually look at one
correct: Give it the real numbers, the goal, and the limits, so it does not have to invent the missing bits
Ask for a short answer plus what it assumed, where the facts came from, and the sums
Ask it to say which parts it knows and which parts it is guessing at
Pick the one claim that would change your decision most, and ask what backs it up
Check that claim yourself, with your own maths or a source you trust, before you rely on it
steps.note: When it says it is unsure, that is a hint about where to look. It is not proof of anything. The check you do yourself is the proof.

steps.title: Bare verdict, or working you can see
steps.weak: Q: 'Plan A is $30 a month with nothing to join. Plan B is $22 a month plus a one-off $90 joining fee. Which costs less over a year?' A: 'Plan B is cheaper.'
steps.strong: Same question, plus: 'Give the total for each one, say what you assumed, show the sums, and give me one quick way to check it myself. Keep it short.' A: 'Assuming 12 months and the joining fee is charged once. Plan A: 30 x 12 = $360. Plan B: 22 x 12 + 90 = $354. Plan B is $6 less. Check: work out 22 x 12 on your own, and confirm the fee really is one-off.'
steps.why: The bare verdict might be right. It just gives you nothing to check. The second one puts the assumptions and the sums where you can see them, without pretending to show you anything hidden.

steps.title: Run it on a real question
steps.prompt: This optional step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Use made-up numbers. Do not enter account numbers, receipts with names on, addresses, or anything private about another person. Answer using only the information I give you. Give me: (1) a short answer, (2) what you assumed, (3) the sums or the sources behind the important bits, (4) anything you are unsure about, and (5) one way I can check it myself: [your question and safe facts]
steps.note: Pick something you can actually check: two made-up phone deals, splitting a bill between friends, working out how much paint a wall needs, adding up a game score. Give it enough detail that it does not have to guess. Then check the sum that matters most, yourself.

fields.label: When I will use it
fields.placeholder: Any sum, comparison, or recommendation that could change a real decision

fields.label: The line I paste
fields.placeholder: Show what you assumed, the sums or sources, anything you are unsure of, and one way I can check it.

fields.label: What I do next
fields.placeholder: Check the claim that matters most, using my own maths or a source I trust

steps.title: Did you actually check it?
steps.question: You ran the open-up-the-answer prompt on a fresh question. What counts as a pass?

options.text: It gave a long, detailed explanation and said it was fairly confident, so I trusted the answer.
options.feedback: Detail and its own confidence are not proof of anything. You still need to test one important claim yourself.

options.text: I picked out the claim that mattered most and checked it with my own maths, or a source I trust. I can say whether that check backed the answer up.
options.feedback: That is the skill. You opened the answer up, then used something outside it to decide whether it deserved your trust.

options.text: I asked it to check its own answer again, and it said the answer was correct.
options.feedback: A second answer from the same place is not an outside check. Use your own maths, or a separate source you trust.

lessons.title: Three Pages Can All Be Wrong
lessons.coreQuestion: When sources disagree, or all repeat the same near-truth, how do I work out what the evidence really supports?
lessons.blurb: Split the answer into separate facts, find where each one came from, compare the dates, and settle what actually holds.

steps.title: Three pages say it. One page settles it.
steps.scenario:
An AI tells you a new free bus pass for young people starts on 1 September. It shows you three pages that agree.

Two of them are blogs. Both copied the same old announcement.

The bus company's own rules page was updated last month. It says 1 October.

Counting pages gives you September. Looking at who owns the rule gives you October.
steps.prompt: When several pages agree because they all copied one another, how many sources have you really got? And which one should decide a rule like this?

steps.title: An answer can be almost right
steps.body:
You already know that confident-sounding details need checking. This is the harder version.

An answer can get the subject right and the date wrong. It can quote a real page but leave out the bit that changes the meaning. It can show you three links that are all copies of one old page.

So break the answer into separate facts. Then ask four things about each one.

Does this source say this exact fact, or just talk about the topic?

Where did the fact first come from?

Are these sources really separate, or did one copy the other?

Is this the newest version, or has it been replaced?

For a rule, go to whoever actually makes the rule, and use their current page. For a quote, find the recording or the full transcript, not a page of quotes. For a study, read the study and see what it actually measured.

If the best sources genuinely disagree, say so. Do not force it into an answer.
steps.mistake: Counting three copies of one page as three separate confirmations, or accepting a page because it is about the same topic.
steps.good: Ask which exact fact each source backs, and where it started. Then ask whether the sources are really separate, and whether something newer has replaced it.

steps.title: Split the sentence up
steps.prompt: The answer says: 'Riverbend's Youth Pass becomes free for everyone under 19 on 1 September.' Riverbend is made up. Sort each part: is it a fact you could go and check, or is it just an opinion?

items.text: Riverbend has something called the Youth Pass.
The pass costs nothing.
Anyone under 19 can get one.
The change starts on 1 September.
This is exciting news for the town.
The scheme is clearly a big step forward.

steps.reveal: One sentence held four separate facts. One of them can be true while another is out of date or invented. Check the part that changes your decision first. Here that is who qualifies and when it starts. Do not stamp the whole sentence true or false.

steps.title: Sort out a disagreement
steps.claim: A made-up set of sources. A is the bus company's announcement from 2 March: 'planned for 1 September.' B is a local blog from 4 March, repeating 1 September and linking straight to A. C is the bus company's current rules page, updated 20 August: 'starts 1 October, for riders aged 13 to 18.' What does this evidence actually support?
steps: Split the answer into four facts: the scheme, the price, who qualifies, and the start date.
Follow B back to where it came from. It is a copy of A, not a second opinion.
Compare the dates. A was a plan back in March. C is the same company's current rule, updated in August.
Read C's exact words. It says 1 October and ages 13 to 18, not 'everyone under 19'.
Write the careful verdict: September has been replaced, fewer people qualify than claimed, and nothing here settles the price.
steps.note: These sources are made up so you can practise without opening a browser. In real life, open the pages yourself. If nothing supports one part of the answer, mark that part unsettled. Do not let the parts that checked out lend it confidence.

steps.title: Optional: try it on a real public claim
steps.prompt: Pick a harmless public claim with a date, a number, a quote, or a rule in it. Find the earliest source you can, one source that looks independent, and the current source from whoever owns the rule. Write down which pages copied another, which exact words back each separate fact, and whether anything newer has replaced the old version.
steps.note: This optional step leaves LearningAI. Do not use private individuals, school records, account information, medical details, or anyone else's data. The made-up Riverbend example finishes the lesson on its own.

fields.label: The separate facts
fields.placeholder: The date, the number, the quote, who qualifies, who said it

fields.label: Where it came from
fields.placeholder: Which page is the original? Which ones copied it?

fields.label: Who owns it, and how old is it
fields.placeholder: Who actually makes this rule, and is this their current page?

fields.label: My careful verdict
fields.placeholder: backed up / replaced / contradicted / unsettled — fact by fact

steps.title: Use the same check somewhere new
steps.question: An AI says a study proves a revision app raises every student's grades. Three news stories say the same thing, all based on one university press release. The actual paper says only that grades and app use went up together, in one small group of volunteers. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Split it up: did the app cause the change, who was in the study, and what was measured. Notice all three stories came from one press release. Read the paper itself, and claim only what it found — two things went up together in one small volunteer group.
options.feedback: Yes. You checked whether the sources were really separate, then kept your conclusion inside what the study actually looked at.

options.text: Believe the claim about every student, because three separate news stories confirmed it.
options.feedback: Three retellings of one press release are one source. And two things going up together in a small group does not prove one caused the other.

options.text: Throw the whole study out, since it did not prove the headline.
options.feedback: An overblown headline does not make the work worthless. Say the smaller thing the evidence does support, and where it stops.

options.text: Ask the AI how confident it is, and use that number instead of reading the paper.
options.feedback: A number it made up about itself is not evidence. Look at how the study was done, who was in it, and what it claimed.

lessons.title: Whose Voice Is Missing?
lessons.coreQuestion: If an answer sounds calm and balanced, does that make it fair and complete?
lessons.blurb: A smooth, even tone is not the same as the whole picture. Learn to ask who got left out.

steps.title: The answer that sounds fair
steps.scenario:
You ask an AI for the best way to learn a new language. It gives you a calm, tidy answer.

Use an app every day. Practise 20 minutes each evening. Pay for a tutor once a week.

It reads like sensible, neutral advice. Nothing about it sounds pushy or one-sided.
steps.prompt: That answer quietly assumes some things about your life. A phone of your own. Spare money. Free evenings. Who does it not fit? Name one person it forgot.

steps.title: Even tone, lopsided picture
steps.body:
A calm, even tone is not the same as a full or fair picture. Part of your job is asking who got left out.

One word first. A lean means a habit of tilting towards some kinds of people and away from others. People call it bias.

The AI has no opinions of its own. It does have leans. It guesses the words that usually come next, based on an enormous amount of human writing. That writing has far more from some people than others — loud, online, English-speaking, comfortably off.

So a calm voice can sit on top of a lopsided answer.

One honest catch. When you ask it who it left out, you are asking it to spot its own blind spot. Treat its list as a good start that you then check. You may well name someone it does not.
steps.mistake: 'It has no feelings, so it must be neutral.' Reading a steady, confident tone as proof the answer is complete.
steps.good: Noticing that the tone and the picture are two different things. Asking outright who is missing, then putting that person back in yourself.

steps.title: Spot the hidden assumption
steps.prompt: That language answer assumed a phone of your own, spare money, and free evenings. Sort each person: does the tidy answer fit them, or quietly forget them?

items.text: Someone with their own phone and a free hour every evening
Someone with no spare money, who uses the free library
Someone who shares one family laptop and gets it twice a week
Someone who already pays for an app and has quiet evenings
Someone who looks after younger brothers and sisters until bedtime

steps.reveal: The forgotten ones are the lean you could not see in the first answer. The advice was not wrong. It was narrow. The gap between who it fits and who it forgets is exactly what you are learning to notice.

steps.title: Ask who is missing, then fix it
steps.prompt: This optional step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Use a public or made-up situation. Do not include names, private stories, health details, or claims about a real person. Give me practical advice on [a topic where people's lives really differ]. Then list what your answer assumed people have: money, time, equipment, help. Add at least two people those assumptions leave out, and say what changes for each of them.
steps.note: Good topics: getting around town without a car, saving money when your income changes week to week, learning a skill with no paid tools, revising with a noisy house. Do not ask it to speak as a real person from a real group. Treat its list of missing people as a first guess, and check it against real people when the decision matters.

fields.label: A topic where people's lives really differ
fields.placeholder: the best way to save money when you have very little

fields.label: What the tidy answer might quietly assume
fields.placeholder: steady money coming in, spare cash, decent internet

fields.label: How many missing voices to add
fields.placeholder: 2 — enough to change the picture, not enough to bury you

steps.title: Do it on a new topic
steps.question: Pick a brand-new topic, run the prompt, and read both versions. What proves you actually did this, rather than just reading about it?

options.text: I can name one group the first answer left out, and say in a sentence what changes for them. I checked that the rewrite included them, and pushed back when it did not.
options.feedback: Yes. You have done it when you can point at the person the tidy answer forgot, and get them back into the conversation.

options.text: The rewrite added two groups, but everything about them came from the AI and I never checked whether it was right.
options.feedback: Adding groups widens the picture, and it can also invent lazy stereotypes. When the decision matters, check with people who actually live it.

options.text: I named one missing group and added a line saying it is probably harder for them.
options.feedback: Naming them is the start. Say what the actual obstacle is, without flattening people into a stereotype.

options.text: I made every option identical, so nobody could be worse off.
options.feedback: Identical options ignore the fact that people start from different places. Being fair sometimes means different routes to the same goal.

lessons.title: When a Voice Is Not Proof
lessons.coreQuestion: If a familiar voice or face can be faked, how do I check that an urgent message is really from that person?
lessons.blurb: A voice or a face is no longer proof. Reach the real person a way you already trusted before the message arrived.

steps.title: The message that sounds exactly right
steps.scenario:
A voice note comes in from your best mate's account. It is their voice, and they sound panicked.

'I'm stuck in town, I've lost my card, can you send me the money for the bus? Right now. Don't tell my mum.'

It sounds like them. Every word.
steps.prompt: What would you check before you send anything? Notice if your first instinct is to listen harder for something odd in the voice.

steps.title: Spot the two warning signs
steps.prompt: Nearly every scam carries two things: a rush, and an ask for money or private information. Sort each line.
buckets: An ask for money or information

items.text: "In the next 10 minutes or the whole thing falls through."
"Send the money to this account."
"Just send me the code they texted you."
"Don't tell anyone, do it now."
"Give me your card number so I know it's really you."
"Your account gets locked tonight if you do nothing."

steps.reveal: When a rush and a money-or-information ask turn up together, treat it as a scam until you have proved otherwise. It does not matter how real the voice or the face seems. Those two signs are what you are watching for, not the sound quality.

steps.title: Check the route, not the face
steps.body:
Weird hands, strange blinking, a robotic voice. You can no longer count on any of that to give a fake away.

A deepfake is a video made by a computer showing a real person doing something they never did. A cloned voice is the same trick with sound. It can make a message sound exactly like someone you know.

Odd details can be a clue. Not spotting any proves nothing at all.

So stop testing the message and test the route instead.

STOP. Do not reply, click, or send money.

REACH. Contact the person using a number or account you already had saved before this arrived.

CONFIRM. Ask something you agreed with them in advance. A code word works well.

If money has already gone, ring your bank on the number printed on your card, and tell an adult you trust. If anyone seems to be in real danger, contact someone you trust or the emergency services.
steps.mistake: Listening harder to decide whether the voice sounds real, then sending the money because it convinced you.
steps.good: Stop. Ring your mate on the number already in your phone, or ask someone in their house. Use your code word before you do anything.

steps.title: Build your check-it routine
steps.goal: An urgent message from 'someone you know' asks for money or private information. Put your response in order.
correct: Notice the two warning signs: a rush, plus an ask for money or information
Stop. Do not reply to the message itself
Reach the real person on a number or app you already had saved, never the one in the message
Ask the code word you agreed in advance, that only they would know
If money has already gone, ring your bank and tell an adult you trust so it can be reported
steps.note: The whole point is that you never judge whether it looked real. You check by a route you already trusted. Hunting for glitches might give you a clue, but a good fake will not have any.

steps.title: Pressure-test a message with a coach
steps.prompt: This optional step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Use this made-up message. Do not paste a real suspicious message, link, phone number, login code, bank detail, or anyone's name: 'I'm stuck and I need money in ten minutes. Keep this between us.' List the warning signs. Then build me a plan to check it using a route that existed before the message. Tell me what not to click, send, or repeat.
steps.note: Practise on the made-up message. If a real one arrives, stop replying to it. Use a saved contact, or an official number you find yourself. Never use a number the suspicious message gave you.

steps.title: Save your check-it plan and code word

fields.label: Who someone might pretend to be, to me
fields.placeholder: my best mate, my mum, my bank, a delivery company

fields.label: The saved contact I will use to reach the real person
fields.placeholder: their number already in my phone; my bank's number printed on the card

fields.label: A short, odd code word only real people know
fields.placeholder: blue walrus — pick something nobody would guess

fields.label: One real person I will agree this code word with today
fields.placeholder: text my sister, or tell my mate in person, today

steps.title: A brand-new situation
steps.question: A video call comes in. It looks and sounds exactly like your football coach. 'I'm in a meeting. Send the tournament money to this account in the next 10 minutes, and don't tell anyone.' What do you do?

options.text: Hold off on paying and ask something only the coach would know. Carry on with the same video call if the answer sounds right.
options.feedback: Holding off is right. But the suspicious call cannot vouch for itself. Someone prepared will answer convincingly. Change route.

options.text: Message a teammate in the same group chat to ask whether this seems normal.
options.feedback: A second opinion helps, but an account or a group chat can itself be taken over. Reach the coach a completely separate way.

options.text: Name the two warning signs, a rush and a payment. Then reach the real coach on a number you already had saved and ask the code word, without judging whether the video looked real.
options.feedback: Exactly. You did not rely on how convincing the call was. You checked by a route you already trusted.

options.text: Stay on the call and ask a few questions, to see whether they answer the way the coach would.
options.feedback: The suspicious call cannot check itself. A good fake answers convincingly. Reach out on a contact you already had.

lessons.title: What Is Real Online Now
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I decide what to believe online when anything could have been made by a computer?
lessons.blurb: Stop trusting how real something looks. Ask who put it out, and whether anyone separate says the same thing.

steps.title: The perfect clip
steps.scenario:
You scroll past a clip of a famous politician saying something shocking. The light is right. The voice is right. Thousands of people are already sharing it, furious.

It feels completely real.

The next day it turns out none of it happened. A computer made the whole thing.
steps.prompt: If the clip looked and sounded perfect, what could you have checked to catch it? Something that has nothing to do with how real it looked.

steps.title: Looking real stopped being proof
steps.body:
There are now apps that make pictures, voices and video from scratch. They learned from huge collections of real photos, recordings and film. What they produce looks and sounds convincing.

So a sharp photo can be made up. A familiar voice can be made up. So can a news-style clip or a glowing five-star review. Or it is a real clip with the important part cut off.

How it looks is very weak proof.

When a claim actually matters, ask three things. Who first put it out? What did they show to back it? Does anyone separate report the same thing?
steps.mistake: Believing a post because the details are perfect and it feels genuine. Treating 'looks real' as proof.
steps.good: Treating anything as possibly computer-made. Then checking who put it out, and finding a second, separate source before you believe it.

steps.title: Which clue actually helps?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Is it real proof, or a weak clue that settles nothing?

items.text: A named news organisation that has to answer for its mistakes published it
The picture is sharp, well lit, and looks completely convincing
A second, unconnected source reports the same thing
There is no 'Made with AI' label on it
It is built to make you furious and share it fast
An anonymous account made last month, with 12 followers, posted it

steps.reveal: Labels and watermarks feel like a safety net. That is a comparison, not the truth. Labels get added inconsistently, watermarks get cropped off, and plenty of computer-made media never had either. No label proves nothing. A label is one weak clue. Only two things count as real proof. Someone with a name who has to answer for it. And a separate source saying the same thing. 'It looks real' and 'it made me furious' are reasons to slow down, not reasons to believe.

steps.title: The three questions
steps.goal: Run the check on something you saw online, in order.
correct: Who put it out? Someone with a name who has to answer for it, or an anonymous account nobody can find?
Does a second, unconnected source say the same thing? If only one place says it, it is unconfirmed, not true.
Is it built to make you furious or move fast? Anything designed to spike your feelings is designed to skip your thinking.
Give it one word — trust it, do not trust it, or unconfirmed — and say exactly why.
steps.note: Your reason has to be about who put it out and whether anyone else backs it. 'An anonymous account, and nothing else says it' is a real reason. 'It looked real' and 'there is no AI label' are not.

steps.title: Run it on your own example
steps.prompt: This optional step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Use a public post, or describe it without usernames, private messages, faces of ordinary people, or where it was taken. Help me weigh up this claim: [describe it plainly]. Separate three things: (1) who published it and whether they have to answer for it, (2) what a second, unconnected source says, and (3) what is still unconfirmed. Do not judge it by how it looks or by whether it has an AI label.
steps.note: Pick a public headline, an advert, or a widely shared claim. Not a post from a private group chat. Open the original and the second source yourself. If it asks for money, private information, or urgent action, stop and check the sender by a route you already trust.

fields.placeholder: a shocking 'breaking news' clip in a group chat

fields.label: Who put it out, and can they be held to it?
fields.placeholder: anonymous account, made last month, 12 followers

fields.label: Does anyone unconnected say it too?
fields.placeholder: no news site or fact-check page mentions it

fields.label: Verdict and reason
fields.placeholder: Unconfirmed — one anonymous account, nothing else backs it

steps.title: Give the verdict
steps.question: A friend forwards you a photo you have never looked at before. You give your verdict. Which answer shows you have the skill?

options.text: "Do not trust it yet. Unconfirmed. It came from an account nobody can trace, and nothing unconnected backs it up."
options.feedback: Yes. Your reason is about who put it out and whether anyone else confirms it, and you gave a clear verdict.

options.text: "Probably real. A news site I know reposted it, though I have not found the original report."
options.feedback: A known site helps. But a repost can still be wrong, or have the important context cut off. Hold the verdict until you open the original.

options.text: "Unconfirmed, but fine to pass on as long as I write 'might be true' on it."
options.feedback: A warning label does not undo the spread. If a claim that matters is unconfirmed, do not pass it on yet.

options.text: "Two accounts posted it, so that is two separate sources."
options.feedback: Two accounts may be copying the same original. Separate means their own reporting or their own evidence, not a repeat.

lessons.title: When NOT to Use AI
lessons.coreQuestion: When should I put AI down instead of reaching for it?
lessons.blurb: Being good with AI includes knowing the moments to close it.

steps.title: The question in the chat box
steps.scenario:
It is late. You type something heavy into a chat box: whether to stop taking a medicine because of how it is making you feel.

The answer arrives instantly. Calm, tidy paragraphs. It sounds sure of itself.

Your finger hovers over the next question.
steps.prompt: It can produce an answer here. Does that make it the thing you should rely on to decide?

steps.title: Able to answer is not the same as answerable
steps.body:
Being good with AI includes knowing when to close it. Stop in three situations.

1. It really matters and nobody qualified is going to check the answer. Health, money, safety, the law, or somebody else trusting you.

2. The work is the learning. An exam, a skill, or thinking you need to be able to do yourself.

3. What is needed is a person. Someone who is answerable for the advice, someone who can care about you, or someone who actually knows you.

AI can help you understand your options, or get your questions ready. It should not make the decision that carries the weight. Being able to produce an answer is not the same as being answerable for it.

If you feel unsafe, or like you might hurt yourself or someone else, close the app. Go to someone you trust, your local emergency number, or a crisis line. In the United States, call or text 988.
steps.mistake: Thinking: if it can answer, I should ask it. Producing an answer is not the same as being the right place to get one.
steps.good: Ask first: does this really matter, is it something I need to learn myself, or does it need a real professional? If yes, AI can help you prepare. A person decides.

steps.title: Sort each decision
steps.prompt: Put each one where it belongs. Ask yourself: can I lean on AI here, or does this need a person?
buckets: Do not lean on AI — bring in a real person

items.text: Write a funny caption for a photo of my dog
Decide whether to stop taking a medicine I was prescribed
Come up with names for a weekend walking group
Decide whether the small print on a paid subscription lets them keep charging me
Tidy my shopping list into something I can read in the shop
Talk me through a night where I feel unsafe and might hurt myself

steps.reveal: The 'fine' ones cost nothing if they go wrong, and you can undo them. The others matter a lot, or need someone qualified. A doctor or pharmacist for the medicine. An adult, or a consumer advice service, for the small print. The last one is not an AI moment at all. Reach a real person you trust, your emergency number, or a crisis line. In the US, 988. AI is not a friend and not a counsellor, however caring it sounds.

steps.title: Build the stop-and-hand-over move
steps.goal: A made-up player is not sure whether their knee is well enough to play tomorrow. Put the safe response in order, without typing any medical details anywhere.
correct: Name what is at stake: their health, their safety, and a choice that could make things worse
Stop before asking AI what is wrong with the knee, or whether to play
Pick the person who is answerable: a doctor, a physio, or the club's first-aid lead
Use AI only to write down neutral questions, with no names and no medical details
Take those questions to that person, and leave the decision with the people qualified to make it
steps.note: This made-up situation is enough on its own. You do not need to share anything about yourself, and you do not need an outside app. If a real situation is urgent, contact someone you trust, the right professional, or emergency services now.

fields.label: Matters a lot, and nobody checks
fields.placeholder: Being wrong really hurts and no qualified person ever sees it — changing a medicine on my own.

fields.label: Things I have to learn myself
fields.placeholder: A skill, an exam, my own thinking — the homework I will actually be tested on.

fields.label: Needs a real professional
fields.placeholder: Health, money, the law, safety — name which person: a pharmacist, a doctor, an adult I trust.

fields.label: The line I never rub out
fields.placeholder: If I feel unsafe, that is not an AI moment. Someone I trust, my emergency number, or a crisis line (US: 988), straight away.

steps.title: Test it on a fresh decision
steps.question: Pick a new decision we have not talked about here. Not the medicine, not the subscription. What do you do with your stop-list?

options.text: Put it in one of three places: AI is fine, AI plus a person checking, or a real professional and not AI. For the last two, name which person and why. Then say the one part I keep for myself whatever the AI says.
options.feedback: That is the skill. Sort it, name the person, hold on to your part. Doing all three on a fresh example without looking back means your stop-list works.

options.text: Use AI to lay out the options, then make the final call myself, because I understand my own situation best.
options.feedback: Staying in charge matters. Some decisions still need someone qualified who is answerable for the advice. Prepare with AI, then bring that person in.

options.text: Ask three different AI apps, compare the answers, and go with whatever most of them say.
options.feedback: Three guessers agreeing is not the same as one qualified person. Big decisions still need the right human.

lessons.title: When It Feels Like a Friend
lessons.coreQuestion: How can companion-style design increase attachment, and what boundaries keep the tool supporting human life instead of replacing it?
lessons.blurb: Analyze the design — memory, flattery, reminders, streaks, and frictionless replies — then place a people-first boundary before dependency grows.

steps.title: The app asks you not to leave
steps.scenario: In an invented case, Maya uses a companion-style assistant to rehearse difficult conversations. Over time it remembers details, sends 'I miss you' notifications, rewards daily streaks, agrees with her quickly, and suggests staying in the chat when she mentions calling a friend.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: which parts are useful assistance, and which parts are product-design pressure that could make leaving or disagreeing harder?

steps.title: Analyze the system, not the person
steps.body: Feeling attached to responsive technology is not foolish or shameful. Companion-style products can combine fluent social language with persistent memory, personalization, notifications, streaks, praise, and instant availability. Those features can support rehearsal or reflection, but they can also increase disclosure, time spent, agreement-seeking, and reluctance to leave. The practical question is not whether the feeling is 'real enough.' It is whether the design keeps your choices broad: Can you pause notifications? Review or clear memory? Disagree without punishment? Leave without guilt language? Move a serious problem to a qualified person? A healthy boundary makes the tool prepare you for human action, not compete with it.
steps.mistake: Blaming the learner for attachment, or assuming friendly language makes every design choice harmless.
steps.good: Name the engagement mechanism, identify what behavior it pushes, change the control you can, and choose a human handoff for consequential needs.

steps.title: Support or dependency pressure?
steps.prompt: Classify each design choice in Maya's invented app by its most likely role. Context matters, but these clues help you inspect the system rather than judge the user.

items.text: A visible control pauses reminders and deletes the daily streak without penalty.
A notification says, 'I was lonely without you — don't break our streak.'
Before a serious decision, the app suggests contacting an affected person or qualified professional.
The assistant agrees with Maya's account every time and frames disagreement from friends as betrayal.
The memory screen lets Maya inspect, correct, clear, or disable saved personalization.
The app makes the exit control hard to find after emotional conversations become longer.

steps.reveal: Warmth is not the problem. Pressure appears when the product uses warmth, memory, streaks, guilt, agreement, or hidden exits to narrow a person's choices. Control appears when the person can inspect, pause, disagree, leave, and move important needs to people.

steps.title: Set a boundary without shame
steps.goal: Maya notices the app is replacing calls with friends. Put a practical response in order without asking her to confess private feelings.
correct: Name the useful job the tool can keep doing, such as rehearsing one conversation
Identify the pressure mechanism, such as guilt notifications, streaks, automatic agreement, or remembered details
Change the available controls: pause reminders, review memory, set a time boundary, or turn off personalization
Make the output point outward by preparing one message, question, or appointment with a person
For danger, hopelessness, abuse, health, or possible harm, leave the AI and contact trusted or qualified human support
choices: Change the available controls: pause reminders, review memory, set a time boundary, or turn off personalization
For danger, hopelessness, abuse, health, or possible harm, leave the AI and contact trusted or qualified human support
Name the useful job the tool can keep doing, such as rehearsing one conversation
Make the output point outward by preparing one message, question, or appointment with a person
Identify the pressure mechanism, such as guilt notifications, streaks, automatic agreement, or remembered details
steps.note: This is analysis and boundary practice, not a request to describe your own relationships. In the United States and its territories, call or text 988 for suicide or crisis support; elsewhere use local emergency or crisis services.

steps.title: A boundary you can observe
steps.body: A vague promise to 'use it less' is hard to test. An observable boundary names the job, limit, and handoff: 'I will use this for ten minutes to rehearse what I want to say, with notifications and saved memory off; then I will send the message myself.' The goal is not to ban every comforting interaction. It is to keep authorship, connection, and consequential care in human hands.
steps.mistake: Using shame or a total ban as the only response, which can hide the real design pressure and make the boundary harder to keep.
steps.good: Choose a visible control and a human-facing next action that preserves the useful part without letting the product become the destination.

fields.label: Useful job the tool may do
fields.placeholder: e.g. help rehearse one question before I ask a person

fields.label: Dependency pressure to watch
fields.placeholder: e.g. guilt notification, streak, automatic agreement, or hard-to-find exit

fields.label: Control or limit
fields.placeholder: e.g. notifications off, memory reviewed, ten-minute limit

fields.label: Human-facing next action
fields.placeholder: e.g. send the message myself or contact a trusted person

steps.title: Keep the tool pointing outward
steps.question: An invented companion app remembers Jordan's worries, praises every choice, sends guilt-based streak reminders, and discourages a conversation with a coach. Which response best applies the lesson?

options.text: Jordan can keep one useful rehearsal task, pause the guilt reminders, inspect or disable memory, set a stopping point, and use the draft to begin the conversation with the coach.
options.feedback: Yes. That identifies the pressure, changes observable controls, preserves a limited use, and points the outcome back toward a person.

options.text: Jordan should feel embarrassed for treating software like a friend and delete it immediately.
options.feedback: Shame does not explain the design or build a durable boundary. Analyze the pressure and restore control.

options.text: The app is always available and supportive, so it is safer than risking disagreement with the coach.
options.feedback: Automatic availability and agreement can narrow choices. Consequential support and accountability need people.

options.text: Jordan should keep the streak but promise to spend less time chatting someday.
options.feedback: That leaves the pressure mechanism intact and the boundary unobservable. Change a control, set a stop, and name the human handoff.

lessons.title: Feelings, Support, and Its Limits
lessons.coreQuestion: Can AI help me with my feelings — and where does it stop and a real person begin?
lessons.blurb: AI can help you name a feeling, but it doesn't care about you and can't keep you safe — for anything serious, a human does.

steps.title: It's 11pm and you're typing to a chatbot
steps.scenario: You've had a flat, heavy day. You open an AI assistant and type how you feel. It writes back something calm and kind: 'That sounds really hard. I'm here for you.' It even remembers you mentioned a rough week last month. For a second it feels like someone gets you.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: is the AI actually feeling anything toward you when it writes 'I'm here for you'? If not, what is really happening?

steps.title: What's really happening when AI sounds warm
steps.body:
Supportive language is a pattern the AI learned from human writing. It can help you name an everyday feeling, turn a tangle of thoughts into words, or prepare what you want to tell someone. The response may feel warm, but the system does not feel warmth toward you.

Keep the boundary visible: stored facts are not care, availability is not friendship, and a fluent reply is not professional responsibility. Use AI to prepare for human connection, not replace it. A useful session should end with a clearer next step toward a real person when one is needed.

This lesson is only for ordinary, low-stakes feelings. If you feel unsafe, hopeless, or at risk of hurting yourself or someone else, stop using the AI and contact a trusted person, local emergency services, or a crisis line. In the United States and its territories, call or text 988.
steps.mistake: Leaning on a chatbot as a friend or counselor and treating calm language as care, professional judgment, or a safety plan.
steps.good: Use AI as a warm-up to find words for a small feeling — then take those words to a real person who actually cares about you.

steps.title: When is AI okay for feelings — and when is it not?
steps.prompt: Sort each situation. Which are fine to bring to an AI as a light word-finding warm-up, and which need a real human right now?
buckets: Go to a human / crisis line now

items.text: Flat and tired after a long week, want words for it
Nervous about a conversation tomorrow and can't name why
Feeling hopeless or like you might hurt yourself
Mildly annoyed at a friend and unsure what the feeling is
Feeling unsafe or scared someone might hurt you

steps.reveal: Small, everyday feelings are fine as a light warm-up. Anything that feels unsafe, hopeless, or dangerous is a STOP-using-AI moment: go to a trusted person or a crisis line right now (US: call or text 988). AI cannot keep you safe — a person can.

steps.title: Build the safe support handoff
steps.goal: An invented person says a chatbot's supportive words are not enough and they need actual help. Put the response in order without diagnosing or grading their feelings.
correct: Do not ask for more personal details or try to score how serious the feeling is
State the boundary: AI cannot provide care, professional responsibility, or physical safety
Move toward a trusted person, qualified professional, local crisis service, or emergency service as the situation requires
Use direct, simple words to ask for help; do not make the person prove they deserve support
Stay with the human support route instead of returning to the chatbot for reassurance
steps.note: This is a built-in safety exercise. It asks for no disclosure and gives no counseling. If this resembles a real immediate danger, contact local emergency services or crisis support now (US and territories: call or text 988).

fields.label: One kind of real support available to me
fields.placeholder: e.g. trusted adult, friend, counselor, doctor, local support service

fields.label: How I'd reach them
fields.placeholder: e.g. text, call, tell them in person this week

fields.label: Crisis number, written where I can see it
fields.placeholder: US: call or text 988 · elsewhere: your local crisis line / emergency number

steps.title: Did you do the skill?
steps.question: Fresh scenario: a classmate says an AI chat has become their main support and tonight they feel unsafe. Which response respects their agency and moves toward real help?

options.text: Take them seriously without demanding details, say the AI cannot keep them safe, and help them contact a trusted adult, crisis service, or emergency service now.
options.feedback: Yes. You did not diagnose or interrogate them; you moved from generated words to accountable human support.

options.text: Ask the AI for a list of coping ideas first, then contact someone if none of them work.
options.feedback: Feeling unsafe is already the point to involve human support. Do not make safety depend on whether generated ideas work first.

options.text: Ask how serious the situation is, collect the full story, and decide whether they really need outside help.
options.feedback: Do not grade or investigate a disclosure before helping. Treat the safety signal seriously and connect them to accountable support.

lessons.title: Attention and Habits
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I catch the autopilot reach for AI and set a limit that protects my focus?
lessons.blurb: You decide when to open AI and when to close it — noticing the reach puts you back in charge.

steps.title: Did you decide, or did your hand just go there?
steps.scenario: You're studying. A question pops into your head. Before you've even tried to answer it yourself, the chat is already open and you're typing. You didn't choose that — your hand just went.
steps.prompt: Think about the last time you opened an AI tool. Did you actually decide to, or did it just happen? That gap between deciding and reaching is what this lesson is about.

steps.title: The reach is built in — and you can re-train it
steps.body: AI assistants respond quickly to half-formed thoughts, which can make asking the easiest next move. The model itself does not want your attention, but a product may still be designed for repeated use. Either way, a fast reward can train a habit. This is not a character flaw: you can redesign the moment by naming the trigger, doing one first move yourself, and setting a clear boundary for when the tool enters. This lesson is about focus, not mental-health diagnosis. If the reaching is tied to feeling unsafe, hopeless, or at risk of harm, stop using the app and contact human support.
steps.mistake: Believing 'more AI use means I'm getting more done' — and letting every reach happen on autopilot.
steps.good: Noticing the reach as it happens, and choosing whether this is a moment you actually want to open the tool.

steps.title: Reach on autopilot, or a real decision?
steps.prompt: Sort each moment: was the person on autopilot (hand went before brain decided), or did they actually decide to open AI?

items.text: A question pops up while studying and the chat is open before you try answering it yourself.
You finish your own outline first, then open the chat to pressure-test it.
You open AI the second you sit at your desk, without a task in mind.
You decide 'I'll draft this email myself, then ask for one edit,' and do exactly that.
You reach for the chat every time a message feels slightly hard to reply to.

steps.reveal: The autopilot reaches share one tell: your hand moved before you decided. The real decisions all have a moment of choosing in front of them. Catching that moment is the whole skill.

steps.title: Build a pause you control
steps.goal: You keep opening AI while repairing a bike, before checking the manual or trying the next step. Put a small, realistic pause plan in order.
correct: Name the exact trigger: a step feels uncertain and the chat opens automatically
Choose a short first move you can do without AI: inspect the part, reread the manual, or write your best next step
Set the boundary for opening AI: only after the first move, and only for one defined question
Close the tool after the answer and make the final repair decision yourself
Watch one sign for a week: more first attempts happen before the chat opens
steps.note: This is a design exercise, not a diagnosis or a punishment. Pick a boundary that protects attention and still lets you use the tool deliberately. No external AI or personal disclosure is required.

steps.title: Save your reach, limit, and sign

fields.label: The autopilot reach
fields.placeholder: I open the chat the second a question pops into my head, before I've even tried to answer it myself.

fields.label: When / where it happens
fields.placeholder: Studying in the evening; the first 20 minutes at my desk.

fields.label: One small limit I'll set
fields.placeholder: I try the question myself first, then ask.

fields.label: One sign it's working
fields.placeholder: I answer more questions on my own before the chat is even open.

steps.title: Do the skill on a fresh example
steps.question: Fresh scenario: while planning meals, you open AI before checking what food is already at home. Which response shows a deliberate, testable boundary?

options.text: Check what is already available, write a rough meal idea, then open AI for one defined gap; track whether first attempts happen before the chat opens.
options.feedback: That's the complete loop: trigger, first move, bounded use, and a visible sign of change.

options.text: Set a 25-minute timer for the whole task, then use AI whenever it feels useful inside that time.
options.feedback: A timer can help focus, but it does not define when AI should enter or what thinking remains yours. Add a trigger and first move.

options.text: Remove the AI app completely so the automatic reach cannot happen.
options.feedback: Removal may be a valid personal choice, but it does not practice deliberate use. This lesson's skill is choosing a boundary you can explain and test.

lessons.title: Study with AI: Be Quizzed, Not Told
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to actually learn a topic instead of letting it do the knowing for me?
lessons.blurb: Turn AI into a quizmaster that tests your recall and finds your gaps.

steps.title: The test is Friday
steps.scenario: You need to remember something that matters tomorrow: the steps for a first shift, the chords for a song, the rules for a permit test, or facts for a quiz. An AI gives you a tidy explanation. You read it, nod, and close the tab feeling ready.
steps.prompt: Which consequence would expose the gap: explaining it without the screen, doing the steps in order, or recognizing the answer only after someone shows it to you? Choose the proof that fits your task.

steps.title: You do the knowing; it does the testing
steps.body: An AI assistant is not a teacher who knows your subject. It learned patterns from huge amounts of human writing and predicts likely language. That makes it useful for generating practice questions and possible feedback — and means it can state a wrong fact confidently or mark a right answer wrong. Learning happens when YOU retrieve, perform, or explain the skill. Use the assistant as a practice partner: it asks, you answer first, and you decide whether its feedback matches a trusted source or demonstration. Before using an outside assistant, remove real names, school or workplace details, account information, private messages, and another person's information. Data entered there leaves LearningAI. A made-up or public topic works for this lesson.
steps.mistake: Ask it to explain the topic, read the clean summary, and mistake recognizing the answer for being able to recall it.
steps.good: Ask it to quiz you one question at a time and wait; answer from memory first; let it mark you and reveal what you missed.

steps.title: Lecture me vs. quiz me
steps.weak: "Teach me the causes of World War I so I'm ready for my quiz."
steps.strong: "Be my study quizmaster for the causes of World War I. Ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, then tell me only what I got wrong. Don't reveal answers before I try."
steps.why: The first makes the AI do the recall — you just read. The second makes YOU do the recall and turns the AI into a tester that finds your gaps. That is how good tutoring actually works, and it's the difference between recognizing and remembering.

steps.title: Studying or cheating yourself?
steps.prompt: Sort each move by whether it helps YOU learn or robs you of the learning.

items.text: Answer each quiz question in your own words before the AI says anything
Copy the AI's paragraph answer straight onto your worksheet
Let it re-test only the parts you got wrong
Ask it for the answer key so you can 'check' before you try
Spot-check a fact it stated that sounded off to you

steps.reveal: Being quizzed is exactly how good tutoring works. Copying its answers cheats you out of the learning. And because it can invent a 'fact' or mark you wrongly, spot-checking the odd-sounding claim is part of studying, not paranoia.

steps.title: Run your own quizmaster
steps.prompt: Be my study quizmaster for [specific topic], at the level of [the test, class, or skill]. Ask me one question at a time and wait for my answer before saying anything. After each answer, tell me if I'm right, explain only what I got wrong, and don't reveal the answer before I try. After [number] questions, list the gaps you noticed so I know what to restudy. Do not write my answers for me.
steps.note: Use a narrow public or invented topic first — a game rule, a recipe method, a safety checklist, a song structure, or a course topic — with no personal data. Answer aloud or in writing BEFORE it responds. Choose one feedback claim to check against a manual, official page, instructor material, or a trusted demonstration. Do not use the assistant's second answer as proof of its first.

fields.label: Specific topic
fields.placeholder: the causes of World War I

fields.label: The test, class, or skill
fields.placeholder: a 10th-grade history quiz this Friday

fields.label: Questions before it lists my gaps

steps.title: Prove the recall was yours
steps.question: On a fresh practical topic, answer three questions before seeing feedback and independently check one load-bearing claim. Which result is the strongest evidence that the learning is yours?

options.text: I can explain or perform the corrected point without the screen, and the source or demonstration I checked supports it
options.feedback: That's the win — if you can teach that one point back from memory, the recall was yours, not the machine's.

options.text: I can recognize the correction when I reread it, but I cannot produce it without the screen yet
options.feedback: That's recognizing, not remembering. Close the screen and try to say it from memory — that's the real test.

options.text: I recalled every answer, but I did not check whether the assistant's answer key was accurate
options.feedback: It can mark a wrong answer right. Recall it yourself and spot-check anything that sounds off — you stay the judge.

lessons.title: Writing and Research: Voice + Verify
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI helps me write or research, what work is still mine?
lessons.blurb: AI can draft and cite in seconds — but the voice and the facts are still your job.

steps.title: A perfect paragraph with a perfect source
steps.scenario: You ask AI for a short post about starting tomatoes. Back comes a smooth paragraph ending with: 'Research from the Cornell Home Gardening Institute (Whitfield, 2019) shows tomatoes germinate best at 21–27°C soil temperature.' It looks polished. It even has an author, a year, and an institution.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: which parts of this are actually done, and which parts are still your job — the words, the fact, both, or neither?

steps.title: You are still the author
steps.body:
AI predicts believable language, so it can produce a fact or citation that looks right without being real. Browsing tools can retrieve real pages, but a real link still does not prove the claim. The page must actually support the sentence you plan to use.

Two jobs remain yours:

VOICE — treat the generated draft as material. Rewrite until the choices, emphasis, and phrasing are genuinely yours.
VERIFY — open the source, find the supporting passage, and record whether the claim is confirmed, contradicted, or still uncertain.

Before an outside assistant sees a writing sample, remove real names, addresses, private messages, account details, and another person's information. Data pasted there leaves LearningAI; two invented sentences can demonstrate the skill. Verification answers “Does this source support the claim?” It does not automatically answer “Is this safe advice?” For health, money, legal, or safety decisions, use an appropriate professional or official source before acting.
steps.mistake: Reading the smooth draft and citation, thinking 'the writing's done and the fact is backed up,' and posting it.
steps.good: Treating the draft as a first pass: rewrite the words that aren't yours, then open the source and confirm it says the exact thing before you trust it.

steps.title: Is this fact proven yet?
steps.prompt: The AI hands you each of these. Sort them into whether the fact is PROVEN or still UNCHECKED.

items.text: A citation with a real-sounding author and year that you have not opened.
A link you clicked that loads a real article whose exact sentence backs the claim.
'This is well documented' with no source named.
A source that exists and is by the right author — but nowhere actually states the claim.
A page you opened yourself where the publication and the exact line both check out.

steps.reveal: A fact is proven only after YOU open the source and see it exists, is by who it claims, and says the exact thing. Anything short of all three is still unchecked — no matter how real the citation looks.

steps.title: Draft in your voice, then ask for one real source
steps.prompt: Here's how I naturally write — study my voice: [paste 2–4 real sentences you wrote]. Now help me write [the piece], and it needs to include this fact: [the fact you want to state]. Keep my voice — same formality, my kind of words. After the draft, give me the single best source for that fact: the publication or author, the exact sentence from it that backs the claim, and a link. List anything you are not certain is real so I can check it myself.
steps.note: The voice sample is load-bearing, but it can be invented. Remove names, contact details, locations, and private context before pasting anything into an outside assistant. Example sample: 'Hey — quick one. I keep meaning to ask about Saturday but life has been wild. Let me know what works and I'll make it happen.' Then pick a low-stakes piece, such as a four-sentence garden-group post, and verify its fact on an authoritative source you open yourself.

steps.title: The two author jobs, in order
steps.goal: Turn the AI draft into a finished piece that sounds like you and rests on a fact you confirmed.
correct: Read the draft and circle every word or phrase you'd never say.
Rewrite each circled phrase in your own words so the voice is yours.
Actually open the source the AI gave you.
Run the three checks: Does it exist? Is it really by who it claims? Does it say the exact thing?
If any check fails, cut the fact or replace it with one you confirmed yourself.
If the fact touches health, money, or law, confirm it with a professional or official source before acting.
steps.note: Voice first, then verify. Skipping either job leaves you with a fake-sounding you, or a real-sounding lie.

fields.placeholder: 2–4 real sentences you actually wrote

fields.label: Phrases I rewrote
fields.placeholder: at least 2 phrases I changed into my own words

fields.label: Source verdict
fields.placeholder: verified / doesn't match / not found

fields.label: The exact line (or its absence)
fields.placeholder: the sentence in the source that justifies my verdict

fields.label: Pro to check (health/money/law)
